At first the Austrian Government was effusive in ite apparent liberality towartis every section and province of the nopiro bet as the revolutionary shock expended itself. the chief end of that Government became yet inure ob.. lutist, and the means it employed were the sowing of dissen- sions, especially between the Magyars and the Croats, in Hungary. The policy was too successful. While speaking peace to the Magyars, who 11.1 unwieely insist.' on the use of their own language only in the Diet, the Court at Vienna secretly inflamed the tfamions of the Croat, and in the end openly countenanenl the march of Jeßacine', the Ban of Croatia, on the Hungarian capital. Thii awl other treacher- OOP proce.lings drove the Magyars to despair, and ultimately Korrouth and some of the more ardent spirita proclaimed a Republic. Dealt could not believe in the power of such a form of government to maintain itself in his country, and I therefore. after vainly trying to induce the coutnedlOre Of Jerso.;;L, flee young successor te his uncle Pertlinand on the Imperial Throne, E....dupl. . Coli.?Liatery course, he abandoned public life altogether. With the aid of large Russian army, the Hungariant were, after a gallant resist- :lnce erudite', and a reign of terror under General Hayti. I replaced that of constitutional freedom, for which all had , been risked and seemingly lost. The triumphal progress of ' the exiled Koesuth through England end the United Stftes showed, however, how truly free nation, had sympathised with the race he had struggled for, whether under Mon- archical or Republimn form. The atom of the attempt of Francis Joseph to carry on the governnient in the oppresses' kingdom In told with great mre and detail in this volume. In time it was found expedient to loolien the Londe at first drawn, and if possible to er'n back the alienated loyalty and affection eta people naturally most loyal. Al every step the Imperial adviwrs at Vienna tonna one moo in theii path could Dedk only be induced to sanction their changes of police, as each succeeded the other, they felt that their aim weela be accomplightel. But it wag vain to offer to this quiet, imperturbable leader of an unfortunate nation any- thing lrys than the righte of which Hungary had heen robbed; and the time at last came when champion and people received the rewartl of their patient resolution. Be. fore thee scene was witnessed which is thug described:— Two or three days after the news of the defeat at gram had reached thempital DeAk wasetimmoned to Vienna.. Arriving at the palace at midnight, he was ushered at once into the preeenee of the Emperor, who was standing pale and troubled at the window. Presently turning round, he said abruptly.” Well, Deale, what shall Ido now ?" " Your Ma- jesty.- wae the prompt reply, " meet first make peace, and then give Hungary her rights." "Will the Hungarian Par- liament gif e me men to carry 00th, war if I give the Con- atitutien at once?" demanded the Emperor. "No," was DeAlt's oll.er,thun faithfully representing Hungarian opinion. in ite repugnance*he WM' MO the whole wherne of policy that it implied. ell," rail the Emperor after a pease, of suppose it mut e 40." The interview nor at an end, and, without seeing anyone elm, Peak left the capital. Peace was made, and now the day seemed not far diatant when the second, and—re it appeared to some—desperate remedy, for the Ills of the Austrian Empire, was to tri.l in good earnest—the restoration of the Ilungerian Consti- tution. But for the moment the held importunity of the Hungarian citizen remained apparently without result. An intependent responeibleMinistry WWI,. conceded ; !lenge,. declined to abste one jot from her original demands; and the Emperor Francis demob yr., still only the King-elect, not net the duly crowned and anointed King of Hungary. Another year was to elapse ere all difficulties were rernev.l. ' Francis Joseph hod, however, after all. learned wisdom from experience and adversity, and under the judicious counsels of Baron Benet, whom he lied called to l,in Cabinet, that scheme of Dual Government which now existo, and which was drawn up by DeOk, received the Imperial sanetion. THE tiOI.I3.IITHS THE FIRST LONDON BANEERS.—Up to elate period in the reign of Charlm I. the London met, chants lemma have deposited their surplus eash in the Mint, I the busineas of which was carried on in the Tosser. But when Charles 1., in an agony of impecunioeity, seized like a robber the £200,000 there deposited, mllinti it a Mtn, the London goldsmiths, who ever Mum 1306 bad been alwaye more or less bankers, now monopolised the whole banking business. tionie merchants, distrustful of the goldsmiths in these stormy tinaes, entrusted their money to their clerks and apprentice., who too often cried, "Boot, saddle and horee, and term" and at once started with their spoil to , join Rupert anti his pillaging Cavaliers. About 1645 the citizens returned almost entirely to the goldsmiths,who now ! gave interest for money placed in their care, bought coins, and sold plate. The company was not particular. The Parliament, 001 01 plate and old min, htd coined gold mid seVell millions of half crowns. The goldsmiths culled out the luxvier pieces, melted them down, and exported them. The merchants' clerks, to whom their masters' ready cash was still sometimes entrusted, actually had frequently the brazen impudence to lend mmey to the goldsmiths at per cent. per diem; no that the merchants were often ac. tually lent their own money, kind hid to pay for the use of it. The goldsiniths also began now to receive rent and allow interest for it. 'rho men below bored their hole, filled it with powder, adjusted the fuse, and then the younger one got into the bucket, that he might be drawn up, while his comrade remained an instant longer to set fire to the train. Then he also jumped in, and gave the signal to those above to wind away. The only man at the windlass rained the bucket and its living load a few feet, and could do no more the fuse would soon reach the charge of powder, the rock was immediately below the spot over which the two were suspended, and instant death seemed certain. There war not a moment to lc., and the younger miner, telling his friend to go to his wife and chil- dren, sprang out, nhile the lightened bucket was drawn rapidly up. The expluaion took place almost instantly, but no sooner had the dust and smoke cleared away than the voice of the noon who had leaped back, as it appeared into the very jaws of death, was heard, and Inc was speedily drawn to the surface uninjured. He said he had just time to say a few words to his Father, throw himself on his back, and place above him a plank that by close by. A long while seemed to hie, to pass before the explosion, which he supposed would kill him, took place, and he lost conscious- nese for a few seconds, but on recovering found that he was unhurt. The fragments of rock had fallen 011 all sides of him, and some small stones onn the plank with whielt he was covered, but that was all. Just imagine how glatl he must have felt, and how he must have thanked God for itiving him !—Little 11,10.

CHINESE IffseßlAlin 131{0.12S.—The peculiar facilities for roguery afforded by the fact that all respectable marriages in China are conducted by means at a go-between, or broker, are illustrated by the following story may obeerve that its incidents were the talk of native Shanghai, and that they were published :et the time. The unfortunate heroine had four husbands in about as many weeks, having been forsaken by every suitor immediately after marriage. Indeed, her hietory hi a curious one. She described as being lair to look upon—according to Chinese Leste—and M every way cal- colated to attract admirers; her feet of the tiniest, her eyes of the narrowest—and yet somehow or other there always seemed sonae obstacle in the way of her getting a husband. At length a marriage brokeress took compassion upon terror rather, sew her way to turn the despised lady to good to- count. She took her home with her, painted her face, and arrayed her in the must attractive of jackets elan could muster. That dressed, the girl looked very well and very shortly a suitor appear.' in the person of a gentleman of some means, who hint Leen left 3 widower and childless. The brokeress—, white ants- they call these ladies in China , —asked him ninety dollars, which lee, enraptured with the , beauty of him new bride, willingly paid upon the spot. The marriage rejoicings passed off quietly enough ; the husband took the fair one home in much satisfaction. But alas ! favour is deceitful, and beauty vain. A vacant stare oils all the reply vouchsafes' to bine by his wife when he :tddressed her ; then she broke into a crackling. senseless laugh, and he found Mat she roomed. Disgusted at being so imposed upon, he packed her again to the person from whom he lead per. charm! her, wide a anted message that lee made her a present of the idiot and the dollars too. Nothing could have aaited the lady's view more elmirably ; and next day the mad lady was al the disposal of thehighen bidder. Th is time tb eappli- cant was a man occupying some small post in a yieron,and he paid bargairomoney to the extent of twenty dollars ; in the meantime, however, a married tiut childlne barber appeared upon the scene, and he bought her for a hendred, winch he !said, money down, anil carried off the prim before the other. The jilted one thereuism abused the " white ant " roundly, And relos.l to listen to leer attempts at a ounupromiee ; a wife he had bought, 31111 a wife he would have, and the one in question happened to be iiarticuPerly to hie taste. The old craw's eyes twinkled. "Bidet wee," she said—or morals to that effect—" wait a day or two longer, and you shall have her back." The event justified the prediction ;the very next day the disgusted barber bundled back the unfortunate idiot, preferring rather to lase na dolLsrs than his fare. The business so far had ;covered ; two hundred and tem dollars lead come rolling in, and another Inter wae hooked already. This man—the yaineW sooner—had meanwhile taken a trip up dee river, in order to present his deveSions at sone shrine at Mon-elms, near Nanking, with a view Do securing success in his matrimonial schamea and, during his :absence, his number-one wife, fearful lict he should liring back a still more formidable rival, clinched the bargain and brought the lady home. Blet she night just as well have purchased 0 wild cat. N. sooner lied the new wife arrived, then her malady took a more serious form than ever, and the house was turned into a perfect bear-garden. The afflicted .d mucholespised lady was summarily packed off home again and married next day to a traveller from the country. who pakt eimilarly heavy price, and did rabid out that he had married a manioc until he lead got her as far as be resi- dence at Hoochow. Bark she came again, poor thing, likes lead penny ; she proisibly found another Mesband the next week; and meantime the lady who had got potentate* of her reaped a golden has-est.—. Temple B." f. A School of Agriculture has been established at Canterbury New Zealand, with the object of affording attolents the oppor- tunity of aoiniring a thorough knowledge of the science and practice of agriculture. The institution is under the direc- tion of Mr. W. P. Ivey, ALR.A.C.,F.C.S., and is situated near Lincoln, about twelve miles from Christchurch. In addition to the ,ghool buildings there is attached to it a farm of SW acres of land of various qualities, from rich swamp pasture land to light and comparatively thin roll overlying shingle.

A case of cruelty to horses has just come under the notice of the Stratford... Avon county police. Junes Bannon, of Great Barr, near Birmingham, owns • farm at Hil'borough, near Stratford-on-Avon. A few days ago police officers visited his farm and found two horses, one at plough and the other harnessed to 3 cart, with several large wounds about their back., and shoulders. The wounds were all raw, and the linings of the collwa were fill saturated with blood to., depth of eight or ten inches. The horses' manes were 3130 clotted with blood that had issued from the wounds whilst the animals were working. It appears that the de- fendant had ordered the wounds to he blacked the same colour as the horses' co., in order that the wounds should not be reddily noticed. Ihe Bench imposed the inset £2 Oa., including costs. Faunal. AND NIONEY LEN DI:IN.—One proof of agricul- tural depre.ion is to be found in the activity of the adver- tising money lenders, who like wolves hovering round a field of battle, in hopes to feed on the dead and wounded, seek to fatten on the financial ruin of the victims of the past bad seasons. By metes of plausible circulars repeatodly sent through the post to every farmer, and by handbills posted in every village or market town, It Is attempted to I entice needy men into what generally proem a veritdble spider's web. The revelations of our courts of law occa- sionally give the public a glimpee of the handiwork of these gentry, and desperate, indeed, is generally the position of those needy farmers who are misguided enough to be caught in their toils.

NOUN lanitrats'Ta AtCD AgnICOLVCRAL Euro., ViOw.—A eery able lecture on "Science, as It applies to Agriculture," lately delivered by Mr. Punchaed, of Underlev, steward of Lord Bective, before the members of the Penrilh Farmers' Club, has beea tollo,neef by others as instructive and interesting to agriculturists. Recently Prof.sor Buck- , master was the lecturer, his subject being, " Government Classes for 'reaching the Science of Agriculture." Review- ing the subject as forming On important portion of the ' Science and Art Deportment, the Professor stated that amongst the other subjects for which the Committee of Council MI Fslo.tion received a suno of money from Parlia- ment yearly, the Science of Agriculture had recently been added, so that now 8,000 climes are estoblivhol in the coun- try for teaching the elementary subjects in the various branchee of science. The lecturer then proceeded to show that for the stiocess of classes on any subject it was rents- tare there should be a sympathising and intelligent local committee, to see after the registers of attendances, to see that the pupils r.eiyed the essmination papers from the Department of Science, and to exercise a friendly interest in the welfare of the dare. The Department or. to the ex- tent of ro, and sometimes even 70 per cent. in the promo- tion of classes, the teacher of which must be qualified either by passing an e.mination in the subject, or holding a certi• ficate of the Royal Agricultural College, or a diploma of the Rood Agricultural Society at Cirencester. He then stated the syllabus, which by lleing thoroughly mastered would enable the student to pass the elementary examination with- out difficulty ; after which he spoke of the future of agri- culture, stating it must largely depend on experiment. He suggested the use of a small patch of land, where thi, could be carried on.—A discussion followed, in which Mr. Tyson, secretary to the Science and Art Classes in Penrith for some years, mid he and other gentlemen did their best to keep them up, but despite their most strenuous efforts they died away, the chief cause being they could not get the students to attend.—A few words having been said by the Rey. FL C. Pattenson, Mr. Hogorth argued that as it was more a lend- lord's thon a tenant's question, it would be well if the owners of land could In induced to co-operate. To form a com- mittee oat of gentlemen, the members of the Penrith Far- mers' Club, would be beginning :it the wrong end of the stick. The land, to grow more than it had hitherto done, had to be enriched. If the influence of landowners could he obtained, the scheme might be successfully carries' out, hot not till then, as they were the parties from whom to expect the funds for the carrying out of such a step. If the scheme promulgated by the lecturer were carried out in that dis- trict it would do a vast amount of good. He hoped the owners of theism! would endeavour to do something in the matter.—Mr. Buckmaster said it seemed to him that there would be a ',wither of the young men of Penrith who would avail themselyee of the clamex if they were encouraged to dote by their elders and their employers.—Mr. Jame'sm proposed vote of thanks to the lecturer, and If,. Thom seconded it. In doing so he slid he thought the subject might easily be:taught in village schools. In Scotland, many a poor lad, through night classes, had received that whieh bad enabled him to get on M life, and to rise in the agricultural world.

A JCDOR S ADDRESS TO MIFF BEATERS.—At the termi- nation of the trial, at the Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, his Lordship directed that the prisoner, John Campbell, 62, shoemaker, found guilty on the previous day of beating his wife with a hammer ; and the pri.ners Daniel McDonald, Thomas Leatherbarrow, and John Gemmed. convicted during tha day of similarly brutal assaults on their wiyeA should be plated in the dock to receive sentence. The prisoners pleaded for mercy. Addreasing them in astern, vigorous, and impressive tone of voice, his Lordship said You four men have been found guilty, each of you, of a crime about as detestable to my mind as can be committed. You have used violence which would be inencasable if you had used it to men of your own size and your own strength, who could have defended themselves and retorted upon you the cruelty you were guilty of. (McDonald : I'm not guilty, my lord. The Judge : Be ashamed of yourself, and be silent.) But it , was not to men your eolualu that you used this violence it was to women, and to the women whom above all the people , in the world you were bound to protPet and be careful of. They may have provoked you from time to time. I dare say possibly they may have done it, perhaps with cause, perhaps without muse : but if they had provoked you to the utmost of which it is poseible for one human being to provoke another, a tenth of the punishment and the wrong you hare inflicted upon them would not have been justified. And you four men ought to stand there particu- larly ashamed of yourselves when you think that the women you have so wronged would have screened you if they could. You ought to be oroughly ashamed of yourselves you ought to think with what aversion and disgust every man in court must look unop you this moment. You, McDonald, I sentence to fifteen years' penal serviture: you, Campbell, to seven year,' penal servitude. You other two—Leather. barrow and Gemmed—have been found gailty of unlawfully wounding only, and therefore I cannot sentence you to more than fiye years' penal servitude. But I do sentenm you to that term, anti regret that it is not possible for me to send you for a longer period.—The prisoners frantimlly begged the judge to reduce their sentences. McDonald saying that be had a wife and five children, and that he had worked for one firm 15 years. hot his Lordship, takieg no heed of their appeals, immediately left the court. In reply h. T. Burns," let me say that under what is known as the Treaty of Washington, United States fisher- men were allowed fore limited term the right of fishing in Fortune Bay. The waters of Fortune Ray being within the jurisdiction of the Government of Newfoundland, certain local laws were panned far the protection of the fish. These laws were in force before the Treaty wan signed, and it is because the Americans consider that they are injured by demonstrations that were made against their right to fish at illegal times that what is known as the Fortune lily dispute arose between this country and the United States. The United States went in for securing an indemnity, 911 d Lord Baliebery, the late Minister for Foreign Affairs, in tie com- munications to Mr. Secretary Evart, took the ground that the local laws should be repealed. Mr. Evart, in reply, held that the list of the fishery articlmof the Treaty showed that there was no limitation whatever upon the grant, ex- oept that the estate, right, and privilege granted were to cod r e only for a term of years, and were lobe enjoyed by the United States, not exclusively. hut in common with Great Britain. Mr. Everts mid further that the paramount consideration prompting the negotiation of the Treaty was the removal of • possit.le cause of irritation arising M the exercise of the fishery privilege, and the result had teen disappointing to the -United State, as he advised Congress to reiinpose the duties upon the products of the Canadian fisheries, as they existed before the Washington Treaty came into operation, until the two Governments be in accord upon the interpretation of the execution of the fishery article, of the Treaty, and for the adjustment of the grievances of the American fishermen. A Bill having this object in view was lately introduced in Congress. .3. M., Altrincham. Vnicamr.

Mr. Henry Vincent, who died last year, was undoubtedly imprieoned as a Chartist. "T. S. will Awl in Moles- worth's History of England, Vincent described as the Demosthenes of the Chartist Movement. The epithet is somewhat ambitiouo. but the fascinating influenced Vincent's oratory some forty years ago was undoubted. Passionately devotml to the cause with which he had identified himself, Mr. Vincent in those days rarely measured hie words, and never scrupled to denounce the leading statesmen of the age. In those days the temper of the nation was excited, and even the Government was not quite calm. Accordingly, on the 10th 3lay, MO, Henry V,neent was arrested on • warrant from the magistrates of Newport charging him with con- spiracy and sedition. Ile was at that hne • member of the National Convention. which was then sitting in London, and which subsequently adjourned to Birmingham. Mr. Vincent , was tried, and condemned to twelve months' imprisonment. it Wan in an attempt to liberate Henry Vincent that Frog, Williams, and Jones comprolnised themselves, and all but forfeited their lives. Mr. Vincent repeatedty sought rands. sion to Parliament, hot without success. The most sotablel of bis efforte to obtain a seat in Parliament was made in , 1844, when he contested the Kilmarnock district of boroughs! against Mn. Bouverie and Mr. Prinwp. The votes on that occasion Good thutm—Hon. E. P. Bouverie, Liberal, 389 ; H. T. Prinwp, Conservative, 370; Henry Vincent, Chartist, 98. Neatly the whole:of thoee votes in support r.f Vincent were obtained in Kilmarnock. Latterly he abandoned all thought of entering Parliament, confining himself to lecturing on the Commonwealth and other general questions of a social, political, ant historical charact„e. Lite in life, Mr. Vincent, without formally joining the Society of Friend., practically accepted the doctrines of that bohly, end with their simple rites he was consignml to the tomb. A brief memoir of Mr. Vincent was published wins time ago, and CT S." will no doubt find much in it to interest tin,. J. lintoos, Widnes.

There is no doubt that the earth it much older than ono gets a notion of from the Biblical account, but our leading astronomers and geologists are not agreed in their notion. as to the exact age of the earth. Professor Proctor the well-known English astronomer, in • recent lecture in America, showed the immensity of Bone. past and future, as revealed by astronomy. From the different geological features of the earth's surface, he said, it has been calculated that 100,000,000 years ha or been consumed in the formation of its crust. Such is tire estimate formed by Crowe and ac- cepted by Sir Chas. Lvell. Taking up the investigations of physicists on this subject. and from experinients by Ilischaff, It is found that the time during which the earth was cool- ing from • temperature of 2100 deg. to 00deg., some 350,000,0 W ymrs must have elapsed. And then prior to this again, there was a long period of time when the earth was ion nebulous condition; en that a fair estimate of the world's age may be placed at 500,000.000 rears. This is considered as erring rather to the side of deliciency than to that of excess. Notwithstanding thin enormous lapse of time, the speaker spoke of the earth as being one of the mod short-lived of the planets. Comparing it with Jupiter, on the principle that the larger a body is, I. its period of cooling will be prolonged. it is calculated that it will be 3,500,000,000 years before the larger planet reaches the stage at which our earth it. Ten timea as long must pass before the sun reaches a similar condition. Actor the moon, it is hat 420,000,000 years ricer she was in this relative period of her existence. The earth will, in 1,000,000,000 years, reach the some stage of planetary decrepitude as is at pre- sent manifested by the moon. The nebular hypothesis of Laplace was then explained. Originally, all the system was star-drift, and then a dense gaseous mass, which assum- ing the shape of a huge disk, began to whirl about ißeentre. As the motion incrmsed and the mass concentrated, a ring of matter war thrown off at the outer edge. This ring in course of time broke up into fragments. After a while these fragments aggregated into one body, and thus the outermost planet was formed. In the same way the inner planets took their shape ; oltimately the great mass in the centre fouled the sun, around which the entire system revolved. himilarlv, in the revolutions of the as yet nebulous planets, their eatellites were thrown off. The asteroids may be considered as fragments which, for some muse or other, never aggregated together; perhaps they were thrown off and too widely Nepal-steel Co come to- gether again. The ages of the planets (in the sense of what stage of existence they have reached) was next taken up. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranue, and Neptune represent a later formation than de those planets nearer the sun. The two former planets. so similar in many respects, are hundreds of millions of years younger than the earth. The rings of; Saturn, it is presumed, will, in time, break and become con- densed into satellites. Jupiter it eurrounded by great masses of clouds of very light density, far within which the real planet is supposed to exist. Coming to the planets nearer by, the moon, with its deep chasms and its great mountains, was described. The dark plains, core supposed to be seas, are in reality the lads of former oceans now ab- sorbed by the lunar cruet. The intense blackness of the shadows east by the moon :ore indicative of the absence of any atmosphere that it might lessons. If an• planet is of the same, or nearly the same, age at the earth, it is Venus Mars is older. Mercury lea great deal older still, and the oldest of all her companion planets, the moon. Ile said that Venus has an atmosphere alcoa .143 dense as the atmo- sphere of the earth, mid must have a large water service. Mars has about an eptal area of land and water, and mast, have an atmosphere. The moon represents what the earth will he in the future. It hie neither water, clouds, nor at- mosphere. Bob, as the earth is eiglisystne times larger than the moon, while it han thirteen tintee as much surface, it will require about 2.500,000.00 ft years fbr the earth to ar- rive at the present condition of the Mo.. FOlkitillg Out this theory, we greatly reduce the number of planets on which it is posstble fur life to exist. In ma solar system we have only the earth, possibly Venus, and, it may be, wome of the satellites. J. HMIS, hi. Helens.

I shall be glad if you will kindly give it • place in "Notes, Questions, and Answers,"—The invention of the coiled spring in the watch dates from the close of the fifteenth century. It is claimid for Nuremherg, then famous for watches, but the priurity is much disputed. Their intraluction into England is equally uncertain. The watch of Abbot Whiting, dating 1556, is of accredited antiquity ; and Count D'Albanne's silver atch of English workmanship is datol 15n. Hen, VIII. had a watch that went fora week; Anne Boleyn possessed another, as well as a small gilt clock, now in Windsor Castle. lilward VI, had in 1542, a " watch of iron." Mary Queen of Scots possessed ndeath's held and it skull watch one in a case of crystal collin.shaped; and another in which& piece of catgut supplied the place of a chain ; hut all these were foreign watches. Queen Elizabeth hail a large collection of watches. A watch w.ts found upon Guido Fawkes; and of this perial is a curious 0:al-shaped watch in a silver case, ornamented with mythological figures. The English watch- makers of the City of London eve incorporated in 1631. In , 1635 the value ofa brass watch was 40s. In 1658 was con- structed the spiral or pendulum-spring invention by Hr. Hooke and improved by Tompion. Next, Juare, by apply- ing the pendulum-spring. added (to the hour-hand) minute- hand and wheel-hand. He also added the repeating move-; cent in watches. Juare also made repeating watches for James 11. and William 111. From 1698 all makers were compelled by law to put their names on sir watches. In 24 wan invented the horizonkal escapement by Graham, who also invented the mercurial compensation.pendulum. At the beginning of the last cintury war invented jewelling the pivot-holes of watches, to prevent friction. Next, John Harrison by his famous chronometer, discovered the longi- tude, for which he received from Earliarnent £30,000. A timekeeper of greater simplicity than Harrison's was that of John Arnold, far which lie and his son received a Govern- ' ment reward of 53,000. Arneild also made the smallest repeating watch ever known, for which George 111. pre- sented him with 500 guineas. The next improver of the chronometer was Thomas Earnshaw ; and in this state it has remained for the last 90 years with scarcely any alteration. J. B. H., Chester.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAIURPAY, JULY 17, 1880.
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

PAM, Sunday—An odictal—Len., dated the 10th inst., ia pabinehed to-day, granting fall remission of the eentences of all the individuals convicted of participation in the surrectionary movement. There are only 17 of the Communist convicts excluded from the amnesty, who, therefore, though they have been pardoned be the tioverstnent, will continue to be deprived of their political rights. The Minister of Marine hue given orders for a large transport to be prepared, to bring home the amnestied ComAunifitA numbering 314, who are still in New Caledonia. About 480, living in different parta of Europe, will return to France, or will be entitled to do no, by virtue of the amnesty. The French national fete to celebrate the destruction of the Pastille opened in Perin on Wednesday, with the p- sentation by President Gravy of new colours to the officere and men forming a deputation from every regiment in the ' army. The presentation took place in the Hippodrome at hongcbani" the Paris racecourse. M. Grevy delivered an eloquent addrese, eulogising the bravery, the patriotism, And , the fidelity of the army. The cheering that burst out at thel I elme of his &damn War taken up by the immense concourse, which thronged the racecourse, the scene IJeing deacribed eel one of interne patriotic enthusiasm. AFGHANISTAN.

A eorrespondent at Cabul states that events are progressing "fairly etell " towards:a final settlement. The Afghans are docking" to Kohistan, where .abdutrahrnan is expected, in the belief that he is going to lead thern against the English; and measures are being taken in anticipation of an outbreak on the Sista', arrival. It is reported that the Sirdar him behaved inn very tyrannical manner in the country between Kkansbad and the Rind. Koosh, where the tribes are hoeti le to him. Numerous complaint, from traders in Turkestan have tern received in Cabal during the week. All trade is stopped, and many 11.3111 have been ruined, their gooin hay- ing Leen seized in large quantities, some of the sufferers being Peshawur merchants. Probably nays the correspon- dent, if Abdurrabman bits to come to an agreement with the English he will sell these goods to Rokbara merchants to raise funds for a Jelled. The advance of Ayoub Khan on the Cendshar road has come upon some of our officials as • surprise. The Prince wan" without money, with the people hostile to him, the rnountain tribes ref wing tu support hi, and one ilaii his army at feud with the other half ;" but them difficulties appear to have been surmounted, and at the last accounts Ayoub was advancing with between 8,000 and 7,000 horsemen and infantry and 30 guns. The following telegram, dated Wednesday, has been for- warded from the India Office .—" Reported from Cabot that Malta Rahman will be close to Charikar, 15th. Much delayed by tad roads and weak transport animal.. The deputation sent horn Cahill meet Sir tar to-day. They write in much hope of satisfactory arrangement, say that there,, no gathering in Rohistan. All quiet round Calm!. St. John telegraphs front camp on Helmond, opposite Girishk, that brigade arrived them 11th, all well aupplim abundant. Helmond fordable everywhere. Trustworthy news has arrived that Ayub's main body was at Saki in Bakwa on ath, , and that Luinab was to turn off from that place with cavalry into Zaimindawur. A spv, however, MAL. that Luinals's main body was two days ago at I silaram, and that his ad. varier guard of 100 men had arrived in Washir. Advanced column of Wall's troops is about twenty miles north-east of tiirishk. Nor Mahosned Khan, cousin of Wall, made attempt to excite mutiny in Wali's troops, and, on failing, left Wali's camp. cavalry gone after AMERICA. '

New Yong, Sunday.—Mr. Thompson, the secretary of the navy, speaking at a alerting at Terre Haut, Indiana, Mid that the right of every citizen to vote would be main- tained at the coming election with all the power of the Government, and would moreover, if necusary, be supported by the military and naval forcee of the country. He con- cluded bin speech by stating that President Haves would be equal to any emergency for the protection of all citizen., be they high, low, rich, or poor. Mr. Garfield, the Rcpu LI icon undidate for the Presidency of the United States, in a letter accepting his nomination, thoroughly endorses the platform of the party. He urges that the rights of the nation should be maintained, rejects the principle of State supremacy, and declares that the election laws should be executed, the rights of electors everywhere protected, and votes honestly COLUIIed. tie advocates the application of the surplus revenues to the payment of the debt, and approves the resumption of specie payments. With regard to the tariff, Mr. Garfield recommends that it should be each as to enable Ameriu to compete fairly with foreign competition. RUSSIA. . .

It is stated that the 'Minister of Justice is engaged in elaborating a scheme of judicial reforms to lac introduced in Siberia, . . .

BERLIN, Thursday.—According to intelligence received here from Bucharest, the Russian Government has made representations to Roumania respecting the alleged toleration of Nihilists in the principality, and has demanded their ex- pulsion. TURKEY AND THE POWERS. In a communication to the Turkish Foreign Minister, Mr. Gosehen calls the attention of the Porte to the delay which him taken place on the part of Turkey in carrying out ore- tale provisions of too Berlin Treaty.. He requests from the I Porte an explicit statement of its intention regarding the Montenegrin frontier. Finally he draws attention to the alst article of the Berlin Treaty, by which the Porte undertook 'to carry out improvements art, administrative Worms in I Armenia. Her Majesty's Government, as one of the signa- tory powers of the Berlin Treaty, demand the complete and immediate execution of article 01 of that Treaty, and call upon the Porte to state explicitly what steps they have taken jto fulfil its provisions. Tho SCIIOII9 attention of the 'Turkish Government is called to the grave responsibility it • would Mcur by any fresh delay. Vlesme, Wednextay.—Two Notes addressed to the Powers I by Turkey have been published to-toy. The first is dated • June =, and the second June BS. In the former the Turkish Government delares that it will never consent to the cession of Janina, Larissa, Aletmvo, and Prevesa. In the second I note it reiterates this statetnent, and maintains that the I cession would have the most terrible consequences, or t..e I inhabitants would resist to the laat extremity.

The attack was made on the 12th instant. The fighting which ensued lasted two hours, and resulted in the retreat of the Montenegrin, who left an officer and twelve men on the deli. The Albanian lost was two killed and ' three wounded. The disparity in the losses sustained by the two parties were occasioned by the fact that the Alban- ians were entrenched behind their fortifications, and the Montenegrins had to attack them there."

div.head: VICTORIA UNIVERSITY, MANCHESTER.
div.p: VICTORIA UNIVERSITY, MAN- CHESTER.

The commemoration of the foundation of the Victoria University, Manchester, has been hekl In Manchester during the past week. On Tuesday evening, a soiree took place at Owens College, when upwards of LOBO invitations were issued. and, as about 1,500 of Mae invitations were ac. °opted, the institution was tilled almost to ifs olmom caw City with a brilliant sod select assemblage. Amongst those who accepted invitations were his tirace the Duke of lievon- shire, chancellor of the Victoria University; Lord Justice Bramwell, Mr. Justice I.indley, the Archbishop of York, the Bishop of Manchester, the Mayors of Manchester, Salford, and Warrington ; the High Sheriff of Lancashire, sors from the staffs of Owens College, the Yorkshire College, Firth College, Sheffield, the Lancashire Independent College, St. Bolt's Roma a Catholic College. Mason's Col- lege, Birmingham, Lincoln College,Oxford, Trinity College, Cambridge ; the Foreign Consuls in Manchester the 1 nder Sheriff of Lmcashire. The following ',Mimeo from this , district received invitations to the wires •—Moore. Wm. ' Armitage, Bowden ; John Aitkin,Crinston ; Thomas Brown- ing, Sale ; Edwin flutter, Bowdon John Brock, Widnes ; J. E. Bailey, Stretford Willhoo Battereley, jon., Lomm J. A. Birch, Timperley ; F. D. Brooke, Bowdon ; W. Bin. yon. Bowdon ; John Crostield, Walton Lea; H. W. Deacon, Widnes; S. T. Dawson, Timperley ; George Falkner, lim- perley; T. G. Finley, Bowdon; If. T. Gaddnm, Bowdon; T. Grundy, Lyinna Canon Gore, Bowdon; William Grim- , straw, Sale ; Rev. T. D. Hall, ; W. H. Houldsworth, linnhstord; Edward Jackson, Bowdon ; Rev. Alfred Jones, Carrington ; F. E. kfatthews, Nanewich William Milne, , Bowdon Mayor of Warrington; John Mitchell, Bowdon J. F. Milne, role, A. Mil/organ, Sale ; A. Mills, Bowdon;; l'ollard. Sale; John Ryland, Stretford; Dr. If. , Simper., Bowdon; C. Sparrow, Urniston; E. Swanswick, I.vmm ; Rev. W. J. Twaddle, Altrinehern ; J. W. Thomp- w;n, Siorthwich H. S. Timmis, Widnes ; James Worthing- ton, Sale; W. H. S. Watts, Fliaton; and E. L. Williams, •Iti:fficham.

The guests were received in the library of the college by the treasurer, Mr. Alfred Neill, and the principal, Professor Greenwood, and they afterwards dispersed through the vari- ous rooms of the institution, where works of net, scientific, microscopic, and other objects of interest were displayed. Members of the professional staff of the college gave brief lectures during the evening, explanatory of various objects exhibited, whilst in the chemical theatre the telephone was used by Professor We and a number of interesting ex- periments with Wilde's electric light were exhibited tiy Professor Roscoe. The movement, which has culminated in the granting of the charter of the University, had its origin at Owens College in 1.75, and the case of the promoters may be stated in few words. The characteristic features of the Victoria Urn- an compared with other British l'niversities will be these.—lt will not, like London, confer ie degrees on can- didates who shall have passed certain examinations only. but will also esquire attendance on prescribed coursers of academic study in a college of the University the constitu- tion of the University contemplates its ultimately hecorning a federation of colleges but these colleges will not be situated, like those of Oxford and Cambridge, in one owe, but whresvera college of ado:mate efficiency and stability shall have arisen. The Victoria Universi.y will therefore be, like the older Universities of England and Scotland, at once a teaching and an examining beefy; and there will be an intimate association between the teaching and the examin- ing functions. In order, however, duly to secure its national character, the governing body will consist partly of persons nominated by the Crown, and partly of repreeentatives of the governing and teaching bodies of the colleges, and of the graduates of the University. In like manner, with a view to the due independence of the examining functions of the University, external examiners will be appoin.d, and all examinations will tre comlucted jointly by such external examiners and examiners representing the teaching body. Owens College, the first, and so far the only college of the University, is a most admirable educational institution. It wee roundel under the will of John Owens, a Manchester merchant, who died in 1916. The capital stun of L 91,000 which John Owens left for the pawner of the institution has grown by successive *umtu to some 6400,000. The teaching staff consistent some 33 professors and lecturers in arts, science, and law, and 10 professors and lecturers in medicine and surgery. In the session of 1879.60 just con- cluded, the number of students in the arts, science, and law departments was 392 in the medical department 232 and in the evening classes 731, making a total of 1,355, or, allowing for double enterics, 1,296. MEETING OF THE UNIVERSITY COURT. The initial meeting of the Court of Victoria University was held on Wednesday morning, at Owens College, Man- chester. The Chancellor (the Duke of Devonshire) presided, and there was a numerous attendance of inembers, including the Archbishop of York. On taking his twat. the CNANCEI.- lA/Et congratulated the members upon the creation of the new university, and especially those members who, earnestly impressed with the urgent teed of providing additional ' facilities for the promotion of advanced education in the Northern counties, had been made imitrannental in directing public attention to the subject, and in convincing the Government of the justice of the Chinn advanced for the emotion of the univereity. When he looked around and saw whom he was honoured in being associated with he thought he would be justified in expressing a confident hop. they will not be disappointed, and that the Victoria Usiye.sity would before long take an important plot- among the uni- versities of the land. Ile concluded by Dying upon the table Ohs Royal Charter, which has Iron signed by Ifer Maj.ty, and with making the formal declation "that this meeting of the University Court constitute. the opening of the university, and the commencement of its labours." (Applatmed Dr. liaszwwoon, Principal of Owens College (Vice- Chancellor), reported various nominations to the Court anal on the motion of the Archbishop of York, Prolmsor Rosen., also of Owens, was appointed pro-Vice-Chancellor for the term of the vice-chancellorship. Tire VICE-CSIANCRLI,R reported that the gentlemen fowl- toted to the Court by the Lord President (Earl Spencer) were the Earl of Derby, tl.e Bishop of Manchmter, the Imean of Manchester, Mc. Thomas Ashton, Dr. Joule. and Dr. Gott (Vicar of Leeds,. A series of resolutions defining the relations between the Court and the Council, which by the charter is made the executive of the university, were adopted, and certain direc- tions were given as to the duties of the board of studies, which is to be formed by the Council. The Council were directed to report to the Court upon a number of subjects, such as the financial arrangements of the university and the regulations as to matriculation. Professor Row ow proposed that until a scheme of studies and examinations should have been adopted Inc the Court, the matriculation examination of the I, niversity of London should be regarded as equivalent to whatever entrance or ! preliminary examination the university might appoint.— Protester Gowns. secmded the resolution, which was passed. The Ergot of MANCISESITH proposed that until the Court should have adopted a jiermanent common seal the cominon seal of the univenrity should be simply the words Victoria University, Manchester."—The motion having been sec; onded,the Archbishop of York moved that the worn" Man- chester" should be omitted, which WAS seconded by Mr. E. Baines.—After some discussion on this point, the Dean consented to the withdrawal of the word, and the substitu- tion for it of the figures "1880." A vote of thanks to the Duke for prmiding brought the meeting to a close. MEETING OF THE COUNCIL ADIrRESS TO THE

div.head: DERE OF DEVONSHIRE.
div.p: DERE OF DEVONSHIRE.

A meeting of tne Manchester City Council was held in the ;Memnon. The Mayor (Mr. Al,lermro Patterson) pre- sided. On the motion of Mr. Alderman ti Runny, ex.mayor, seconded by Mr. T. SCHOFIIII.O, an addrma to the Duke of Devonshire was adopted. Subsequently the members of the , Council adjourned to the banquetting room, in which the Duke and the members of the University Court had as- sembled. The address to the Duke we, presented. In it the Council congratulated his grace upon the inauguration of the Victoria University. It was specially gratifying to them to receive his grace in his noble c ipacify as heed of one of the older Universities and of the newest University, uniting the old learning with the new, and the ancient seat of cul- ture with its most modern form of development 1 while he must be proud of those illustrious member. of his house, a great chennet and a great lawyer, who hod shed lustre upon the teaching of the University of Cambridge. They were well aware of the deep interest his grace took in the metal- lurgical and textile trades, which had enriched the country. The Prom, in replying, said he could not doubt he was expressing the sentilnents of ell the authorities of the Vic- toria University when he took upon himself to assure them in their lehalf as well as his own that they recognised in this address a most encouraging mark both of the interett taken in the University by the cititens of Manchester, rod the confidence with which the constitution of the Univer- eity Court was regarded by them. The eignature of the Royal Charter which called the Victoria University Into existence, and constituted Owens College an integral part of that University, could not fail to have a powerful in- fluence in promoting still further the progress and uteful- nese of Owens College. THE BANQUET.

The Duke of Devonshire and the other authorities of the University were afterwards entertained at a banquet in the Town-hall ; the Mayor of Manchester (Mr. Patterson) pre- sided, and amongst the guests, who numbered about BY), were Earl Spencer, the Archbishop of York, the Bishop of Manchester, Lord Winmarleigh, Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P. Mr. Stagg, MP., Sir Itghtre4 kar-Sbuttleworth, Mr. E. A. Freeman, Professor Huxley, and others. The Earl of Derby and Mr. John Bright, M.P., who had been expected, were
imable

They wanted a charter to grant I medical degrees, the want of which at present was a serious defect in their new organieation. Earl SPIOIOO4. who w. received with cheer% responded at considerable length. He came there, he mid, to show not only the interest which Her alajesty's Government feel in I the movement which had taken such a great step in advance I that day, but specially the interest which the department I over which he had the honour to preside felt in the eaten- sion of higher education generally. It was to his depart. inent the country had committed the dray of maintaing the i highuit state of education in the primary achemea of the country, and in dispensing the now large Parliamentary grants which are yearly given for this admirable object. He was sure they could not enter more deeply into the importance of the subject than he did, or 00, keenly feel the desirability of maintaining the high standard • of education among the working classes of this country. I , without which the people of tho country would be unable , , to compete not only with Scotland, where education had ni • I long maintained such • high position, but with other noun- I tries in the world. When we hope to do is td provide coroner, child in the country the means of education--a eoood practical training. Then we wish to provide a ladder by which the more intelli- gent children may climb from the purely practical education and get the advantage of secondary ochoolt. And we hope by means of exhi bitious and echo! arsh ins they may he enabled to climb from the eecoodary school to Um Universities-- (cheers)—and thus the whole gamut of education will be thrown open to them. Throughout the country there is a lot of work to Le done, but if wr can get hold of the large cell.ea of industry we shall eaaily achieve our object. TUESDAT.—There has always been a great deal of ex- , citement on the morning of the day on which the first stage 'of the Queen's Prize begins to be shot for. Consequently there WAe some little liveliness about the camp some time I before the rerrille was sounded. It was noticed that the authorities were very careful to make the arrangements as I specific as possible. The register keepers received very precise instruction?, from Major Thompson. the head of the , statistical department, who impressed upon them the urgent ! necessity of acting strictly on the rules laid down for their I gredance. Those volunteers who had the time took advan- tage of the pool targets to test the wind and elevation, and the flriag points for this purpose were crowded for • long I time, not a few being rewarded with bull's eve, which well paid them for their outlay. The men from each county were , put to fire together se far as possible. The Cheshire 'volunteers shot at ten o'clock, and the Lancashire men I went to the target. id twelve o'clock. Tee temporary schtiol and nursery for the pauper children of the Warrington Union has turned out to bet • veritable hotbed of filth and disease. Pb: a keg time past the Guardians have devoted much of the time of their weekly u.eetinge to diaputee over the removal of the poor children from the Workhouse to the Mihtte Barra:lke and it roust have lath patent to the public that the greater part of the Board have looked upon the isolation of juvenile paupere pretty much as a hobby, and that they were determined to ride it to the end of the course at all ricks. The stub- boron., with wbich the scheme has been preened forward in spite of warnings of its coetliness and of the unhealthiness A the new home of the children Imo, in face of the dicot. mires made at the meeting of the Guardians on Widen @day lace, little to commend it. At meeting after meeting Major Cartwright Itas protested against the removal of the children from the Workhouse to the Barracks, and rese.era of the Erman., null remeentier that on more than one oath- non the unhealthiness of the Barracks as a habitation haa been urged in the most forcible manner. Conpled with this protestation and allegation, it has been anevered over and over again that there is ample accommodation for the children in the Workhouse ; but the advocates for the isolation of the children from adult paupers by the setting up of a double establiehmeut, and by • conatigneat doubling of maintenthee charges, have ridiculed the emanations of their opponents at the Board eel mere illusion.; and, without attempting to allay by in. gnu what Ind become burning epasetions, they have chosen to stabbornly preen forward. their hobby in thc hope that all would Come right in the thd, rather than manifest a willingness to withdraw their hands if it could be shown that they bad got into a false groove. What might have been antied long ago by an Inquiry, when small miachief had been done and tittle expenditure had been incurred, it has been decided to do now, aince the Board'a own medical offiar has de- clared that fifty out of 039 chi/then are in the hegi,jud with bade covered with three and vermin, and that the Barracks is so infened with diegusting vermin that he would not eleep there under thy consideration. Major Cartwright, who drew attention, at Wedneedey'a meeting, to the abominable condition of the Berracke, reiterated hie frequent contention that there watt room for the children in the Workhouse, and that they onght never to have been retthved therefrom. In the whole of his r'i years' experience se • &earthen, he said, he had iiever seen the pauper children in such a shocking condition, end lie mentioned that some children mot in a healthy condition from idle Work- house to the Barracks the other day were, in the course of a few dove, ordered into the heepital, where, on being thorn of their hair, their tirade were found to be covered with score and vermin. This statement was corroborated by Mr. Wthlfall, thd it was backed by a report of a thee of • " eisrnlarly painful nature" from Newton which had come under the 1264100 of Mr. Hall. The hobby rider*, honorer, tesoned to the old practioe of ridiculing, ithtead of tenting by inquiry the truthfulthee of, the allegthions ei to the condition of the Barrack, and of the children and se to there being room forth: juveniles in the Workhouse. Parts they contended had been magnified; the malady affecting the children war of little moment, it being merely • skin dathse the Barracks, too, were not unhealthy, and there was not room in the Workhouse for the children. The latter assertion, however, was met with elle/of " Question " and " Plenty of room." It the not until Dr. Spinks, the Medical Officer had declared the Barrack, to be infested with vermin and the children to be in the condition described that it wee realised there wth ththe for inquiry into the eon' teatime of the opponent, of the child,oct being de- tained at the Barracks. lathe opinion of Dr. Spinks the vermin has been conveyed to the Barracks in the clothing of militiamen, and there I. no chance of the children getting rid of the dirthee until they are takes out of the Barraulth Now that it ham been decided to have an inquiry, we shall probably learn whether

in the Workhouse the children can he afforded the requieits accommodation, and whether there hoe been any juatification for burdening the ratepayers with the expense of maintaining a hotbed of &lease and of resorting to the experiment of erectiog •emend pauper palace etc cost of teens of thousands. The public may be indifferent to members of the Board dividing thenteelves into parties, and to their display- ing a determination to thwart each other, so long or their childish factious play does not interfere with the tfficieut discharge of the bueinese of the Board, or affect the ratepayers' cashbox ; but when their game of checkmating each ,glice involves such a condition of thing. corbel revealed at the beet meeting of the Guardiane, it is high time that the membere asked themselves what they are about.

Preparations are now being made for taking the census cest year. On Monday evening, Lord EtEfisld introduced into the Hon. of Lords a Bill giving authority to the GoveruEneut to incur the noceesary expenditure for numbering the people on the night of Send ,7, the led April next year. The Go- vernment prep.., and we think wisely, not to in- clude in the census a return of the religion. profeenionn of the people, seeing that much retorte do not afford eatiefactory teetimcey of the status of religion. No nloubt there is—and the f Ect is to be regretted—% vast army of people indifferent to religionte exercinee, and who belong tone particular meet. If required to state their religious oonvictioce, they would, instead of re- turning themselves of no religtoun faith, prefer to declare themselves members Ed come particular body, notwithstanding that they might he no ignorant of, and as carele. about, the dogmas and creels of that particular sect nsa mule. We can quite mad.- etand that many will be ready to join Lord Cranbrook in h. &Ejection to the otni.ion from the ennuis papers of qucetione relating to religious be- liefn. From the census papers of 1871, the coElumn to be found in previous eeneun schediCce relating to religious opiumna wan omitted for the reason that such returns were not relinlEle—a disnatiefaction that arose from a knowlidge of the fati that moot people like to be considered religious, however indifferent they may be to religione ordinances. There is a wide difference between a-king a man who he is .d what he is, and molicit in g in forced icti as to him opinions upon religious dogmas, ant' especially when it is known that a cenniderable number of pigeons resent upon principle any interference with their religious views by the State, and when It in known, als that a large section of the community profess to be members of churches they never vinit. aud whose celigious pre- judices sway with the throng or innline to what society may hold tube reepectalEle." It is simply proposed that the heads of all houneholde Phan make returns on pipers to be left at all hounes of all per.et elnep• tug or etaying in each honro on the night of the 3rd of April next. The information to be given "midst, of the name, sex, age, and birthplace of all in the household, their relation to the bead of the house—wife, son, daughter, eervcet, or whatever their position is, whether niarried, widowed, or tingle, their rank, profe.ion, and busicees, and whether any net blind, deaf, dumb, imbecile, or iri.ne. The enumerators, who will diatribute and collect the census pipets, will have to see that the papers are correctly filled up; an(' where they know that inform- ation is withheld, they are to tupply it to the best of their ability. The head of the boxer will c rnquired to fill up time° papers or cacee them to be filled up. The sehedule will contain eight cohunce, and the questions naked will be arranged in such a simple manner that the moist illiterate can, with the aid of an enumerator, or with the aseistance of almst any child attending an elementary school, supply the informa- tion needed. The cunt of this undertauding will, undoubtedly, be very large, and it is very tempting, when such machinery as is needed for the census in set in motion t•E make use of it for the purpose of obtaining information, be) ond that of merely ascertaining the number of the people in the eottntry, which would he highly prized by logic. Intone. stair:inns, philenthropiste, and others interested in knowing ott much as namable of the inner workings of onr great national life. It in beyond cavil that many ueeful columns might be added to the eight which the Government have de- cided to place on the rel.,ot paper, but it most be borne in mind that each additional column tneana a berg expenditure of .pital, and a consequent per- plexing of illiteratee, be-eides burdening the whedulea with information that would take up a very long time to collate and to put before the public. It is, we believe, intended to have the consus returns published more quickly than those tnade in teeEt and 18; I were. The retune will furnish not only the ' numbers of thaw who dwell in houses, but thaw I whose occupations confine them to boate and ships, tents and ban., or whose employment keeps them' b.y by night. The general resulte of the last cepaes of iB7i wore not publinhed till June, C{7; and the completed report did not get into the ' hands of the nubile until pact the middle of t8;-3. More promptitude will be exacted in respect of the coming °emus, and to securo thin promptitude an efficient statf of enurneratorn is to be provided. Promptness is ail the more neesataary, since the returns will be needed as guide', in the arrange• ment for a redietribution of seats whenever the queetion ef household suffrage in the countiee, which the present Government is pledged to handle, foresa itself to the front for adjustment.

Potato growing is a very important factor in our agricultural industry, and, an potatoes constitute a large part of tho staple food of the people, all chews in the British Ides are necessarily much concerned in the cultivation of this valuable esculent. Since the potato disease first manifested itself in Parr it haa aever been eradicated from the potato fields of the United Kingdom, and periodically it has appeared in ita most destructive form, blighting the crope right and left, and leaving in its train, as in Ireland recently, the most terrible distresa amongst the populace whyec subsistence depends upon the aneyeaeful cultivation of this universal article of food. Numerous remedies and preventatives have from time to time been suggested and applied, but still the disease keeps breaking out afresh, first in this part of the country and then in that. Potato growing has consequently become a precarious occupation, and perhaps in no part more than in the isle of Erin. Parliament haa very properly taken cognisance of the diaearfe afflicting tbepotato, and commissioned a Com• mittee to inquire into the cause and porseible remedies so far as Ireland is concerned. The Committee has been engaged in taking evidence, and Its this evidence is not yet aeoessible in any other form, we are in- debted to the Irish papers for their reports of the committee's proceedings. Hitherto, so farce isknown, the potato rot has belled the sagacity and energy of agriculturists to ascertain the cause of the disease, and no doubt the inquiry bythe Parliamentary Committee will lead not only to the collection of much valuable information illustrative of private expen- meats and opinions that will be useful to potato growers in all parts of Her Majesty's dominions, but probably to further experiments, under Government uperVision, in the production of new varietioe of the 'tuber, nod to the aeloption of same defined principles for cropping and storing improved dames of the potato. The origin and dissemination of the disease are yet limited to the domain of theory, and it is in- teresting la notice the difflerencea of opinion which have been put before the Committee. Professor Bald- win said to the Committee that hie idea was that the disease was originally imported in the tuber from the native home of the potato, Peru, and Mr. Worthing- ton Smith had a theory that the "resting /more " had something to do with the diceemination of the diocese. This spore, he told the Committee, vvas so minute that it might be carried hundreds of miles in the air. There may be some truth in this, and instancees are not to seek of seeds of plants, peculiar to one country, being carried unawarco by pilgrims and armies to other Mimeo and there growing up apparently beenn lyexamined ..e pre ymuch Such oft g e witnesses.ra. who to the disease being of foreign origin, but there is a diversity of opinion as to the disease itself, one eat of theories attributing it to a fungus growth on the tuber and another to a canker attacking the haulm. This opens up the queation of the wisdom of the practice of agriculturists consigning dieessed stalks and potatoes to the manure heaps and afterwards spreading them over their fields. Mr. Worthington Smith advised the Committee that local authorities should be empowered to conipel diseased gallo and potatoes to be destroyed by fire and thus utterly stamp out the disrease. In oppoeition to this recommenda- tion, Mr. May, a Kent grower, lodged Lis experience —certainly • singular one—that diseased potatoes were "far better than sound ones for cattle feeding.' Moat of the witnesses concurred in the belief that fora certain peer at every variety of potato rosiated the attacks of di..., but afterwards lost the power of resistance and became extinct. In a draft report the Committee say that a good variety, with careful cultivation, will not degenerate for twenty years. The variety known arr the Regent. how- ever, has been grown for forty years, but Mr. W. Smith told the Committee that owing to bad selection and ovor-cropping ir had of late become more liable to disease. The evidence of some of the more im• portant 'wit..ee went to chew that there is a eom- soon history for every variety, and that diverse- fication is accomplished by care and skill in cultiva- tion, lour or five and esometimee six years are required to produce a new variety, which in the early stages of its cultivation—a species known as the Champion for example—is rather coarse in quality and lacks that &urinena and mellowness character. istic of the Regent. Potatoea of the facet quality are said to succumb the soonest to disease, and an important feature in the cultivation of potatoes in the choice of certain varieties for &Remelt classes of soil. Changes of eoil have no doubt much to do with the ...eel cultivation of new varieties of potatoes in their e.ly stages. Mr. Nieholl, the originator of the Scotch Champion, says that that variety is beet adapted for • wet or cold soil, and he

think. there is much to recommend in the idea of changing seed from " a lighter to a heavier soil." Mr. Jame. Robertson, of Dublin, told the Committee that "potatoes warn on peat land and tent ton higher Icon, produced the best kind of potato that could possibly he produced." In this instance the recom• mended change is from • wet to a drier soil, and according to Mr. Robermon'to experience it in a beneficial one. Not only is change of roil pro- nounced to be desirable, hut allot change of climate, bat under certain conditions, since American varieties of potetwn have not been found to be suitable to Irish lands. An one means of eradicating the disease, Professor Baldwin suggested to the committee that all one year's crop of potato. in Ireland nhould be gathered on one of the islantin on the Dinh coast and there destroyed, and that then fresh seed nhould he obtained from one of the colonien, the climate of which is much the same as that of Ireland. The immense tenaporary loss that would be occanioned by the adop. tint, of this suggestion is not token into the reckoning in the f.e of the benefit which Professor Baldwin thinks would follow, and he buses his suggestion ou chemical ground.. Potatoes, he contends, never do well unless there is ou abundance of potash in the ground; and soil which has been seven or eight years under grass yields the best of potatoes, as the grass left in the land does not abnorb the potash as the remnants of other crops do. The must suitable artifi- ' dal manure, therefote, is, in his opinion, muriate, or nulphate of potaah, put into the ground iu the early rr7o,ltiocef rt,thll year. The Thte Met vi thin kind aroopnf ,ml:untre maintaila that land will only bear two crepe of potatoes in eight years. Iu support of this theory, ke ntated that in Connemara, where sea weal. which is rich in potash, is mach used an manure, bettercrops of potatoes have been raised thnn in other districts. The Committee was favoured with a variety of opinions as Is the choice of potatoes for need. In Ireland the smallest potatooo are used for sued, eel the great rapidity of degeneration is attributed to this cause. Mr. N icholl stated that he preferred the best potatoes for nerd; and whilst Mr. Robertson preferred middle- nixed potatoes for seed, with good :hope and good open, planted whole, Precursor Baldwin suggested the use of middle-Metal potatoes, cut into sets, with two , ryas in each set, net he found that potatoes planted whole needed land exceptionally rich in manure. That Rio production and eduction of new varieties cannot Ibe profitably undertaken by ngriculturiots single- , handed the committee appears hr be thoroughly I convinced, and we gather that they are prepared to recommend that new varieties mnat be produced either by the combined enterprise of the large potato. growers, working together, with the assistance of snob nocietien as the Royal Agricultural Society of England or Ireland, nod the Highland Society of Scotland, or by tho Government lending annistance. It is computed that there are about 400,000 farmers in Ireland engaged in growing potatoes, and who are per- petually raising potatws from the same node, no if the restourcea of the laud would ever and anon comply with their requirements independent of chemical and climatic c.ditions. One result of the inquiry will be the conviction that new varieties are essential, and what the Committee seem disposed to recommend is I the establishment of farms in Ireland for experiment- ing upon the production of new varieties, that Boards of Gnardiana be empowered to furnish soca potatoes , in persons requiring them, and that so far as England I I and Scotland in concerned subsidies in some form' should be granted from the State to Agricultural Societien. The proceedings of the Committee are fall of interent to agriculturists generally, and it is to be hoped that the Committee's labours will be productive of waiver...a good.

div.p: TOWN TALK.
The Nonconformists of Runcorn have decided to hold a demonstration in co nmemoration of the Sunday School Centenary, on the 10th August, and about 3,000 scholar. will Like part.

The annual Inspection of the Widnes Local Board twirl take place on the 27th inst. As eome of the ratepayers have an idea that the refresbments provided on this occasion came ' out of the rates, it may be ae well to say Brat the members always pay for their own. It is really a little marvellous to see that the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, are at last making a move to provide an hospital for infectious diermees. I hope they will be sacsucceesful in securing a Bite to which objection cannot be taken.

The annual pic-nit of the Widnes Lilwral Association is fixed for Thursday next. The place selected is Blackpool, with its magoirieient extent of sea view and other attractions. I I hope that all enemies of “thegunpowder and glory "policy lin Whines and the district, who can spare the time will endeamur to support the committee M their effort. I'lour readers will be pleas,' to hear th.rt the attempt to i make the pretty thoroughfare at Runcorn known as Leinster I gardens, into a rot de sae is not to succeed. The committee of the Improvement Commissioners to whom were delegated the carrying out of the negotiations with the object of pre- venting this proposal being carried out, have proved success- ful in making an amicable arrangement. Superintendent Williamson, of the Runcorn PJECO Force, has for some weeks been dangerously ill, and his recovery I was at one time considered hopeless. I am gratified to be ' able to shit, that he is 1301 V in a fair way towards TOCOVery.

After all, the Runcorn Commissioners have decided to op. pose the Liverpool Corporation Water Bill, but "in the LOMA." It takes a vast deal of pressure to move some people! At the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardianc, this week, a protocol came up for consideration having for its object the carrying out of a change in the system of appoint. , ing medical officers of health. Mr. Dancer, the Local Government Board Inspector, wae present, and made some I remarks to the effect that "the experience of the London Government Board, was that on the whole the working of the Public Health Act by Poor Law Medical Officers had not generally been satisfactory, and to a considerable extent their private practice had been allowed to interfere with their Poor Law duties. However honourable Oman might be he could not help being sometime, influenced by private feeling in a district where he boil a great many patients. Therefore the Lonot Government Board had considered it the best course for one man to devote the whole of his time to the office, and to have no private practice whatever." There is no doubt that the remarks of the Inspector are marked by sound sense and much knowlwlge of that guest thing called hornan nature, which &poets said was a "rum 'on," and of which our friend Mr. Samuel Slick, of Slink. ,yule, WAS_ such a master. We all know that there see . . . .

medical officers who discharge their duty to the poor Inc manner characterisal by much kindness and delicacy of feeling, bet there are others who cannot be approached without considerable caution, and who, "dressed in a little Lief authority," appear to hace some notion that they are conferring a favour when they are simply doing the work for which they are very fairly paid. I have had more than one opportunity of witnessing the roe competition for such appointments. and I wish thatthe same suavity of demeanour which all who have any influence in the matter of the can- didature meet with at that pericel, distinguishol the success- ful cendirlateafterwards. Some gentlemen of the medical profession, who are known to he as sunny in their manner as the most polite could wish, when they are dealing with a patient who is in a good position in the world, change their style of address instantly when they come to do their duty as medical officers, and to deal with the ratepayers who. possibly, once sor better days, but has, through bitt, nsie- fortune or sickness, sunk into the rank of an out-door pauper They remind one of the tale told by "the Clock- maker," in reference to the respect shown by 3 certain minister to some rich people who joined his congregatien. "Slick" tella it as follows Our congregation at Slick. villecontained most of the wealthy and respectable folk there, and escort powerful and united bo,ly it woe. Well, there came a split once on the election of an Elder, and a body of the upper-cruet folk separated and went off in a huff. Like most folks that separate in temper, they hid it all to conscience; found out all at once they had been adrift afore all their lives, and joined another Church as different from cern in creed as chalk is from cheese and to show their humility, hooked on to the poorest congregation in the place. Well, the minister was quite lifted up in the stirrups when he saw these folks fine him: and to show his zeal for them the next Sunday, he looked up at the gallery to the nigger', and said lie, "Mo brether'n, I beg you yrotit spit down any more on the aisle seats, Joe there be gentlemen there non-. Jist turn your heads, my salde friends, and let go over your shoulders. Manners, my brothers, manners before hockey. Well, the riggers seceded ; they said it was an infringement on their rights, on their pri, ilege of spitt in'. as free men. where they liked, how they liked, and when they liked, and they quit in • body." Thin extreme deference to " respectability "teem, to creep in everywhece ! The alteration proposed by the Local Om-eminent Board will prohthly result in a little more attention being paid to some of those who arc amongst the great arm iy of the poor and needy. I have n my Mao. ings and and outgoings, heard many stories illustrating "the insolence of office." One of these, for the truth of which I can vouch, relates to an officer living—well, I will aty within a hundred miles of the Liverpool . the

identify I particular gentleman, who, however, when he wes the tale in print, will, I suppose, experience a little wholesome disgust for the power of the fourth estate to publish such things to the world. Certainly, such in- otances of disregard for the feeling. of • poor person ought to be made known, if it be only to strike a slight element of fear in the hearts of any other public officials like minded. The poor woman to whom I refer was once in a very fair position in life, but she is at present the subject of a malady which came. a very had running sore. She stated her case to the relieving officer having charge of the district where she lives. :mot he spoke very kindly to her, having known her many yeare, and took her to the medical officer, described her case. said she wane widow, well and favourably known, and he hoped the man of pills would do what he could be her. This advice from the rs. lienirg officer appeared to irritate the medical man, who, in a Myle which I hope he does not often adopt, mid "Oh, we don't want anv blather. I hare no time to wail" Then he asked his visitore into the surgery. The medical eervant of the Own-diens then said, very haughtily, "Well, what is it ? " She told her brief tale, after which the surgeon remarked, "You never was a patient of mine," as if that ha I anything to do with the matter She Answered, `• No doctor, I never was a patient of yours, I,' Mr was always my doctor." Having examined
;Idfl
'thg!7'

the waned, the eurgeon mid, 'I can do nothing at all for you. You had better go where you have been before, alld where you have paid all your money.” The woman then asked if the reliever of other woes mull give her a lotion to take eay the inflammation, but he maid he could not do anything for her. The woman, with a sad heart, then left the place. 'The key to this particular tale is that in the town where the worthy who is the subject of it lives, that there ice etiong feeling between him and anoth, meth.' min who lad mice been the family doctor of the woman seaing help. It spnears that as his brother profeseional was far out of the reach of.any spite on his part, he deter- mined to pour the rid of las wrath upon the widow ! It lis satisfactory to know that this in not a fair sample of the profession, as I know some medical officers who are II revered by the poor for their kindliness of heart.

The members of the Orange Imtly in Widnes, St. Helens Warrington, and elsewhere have this week been holding high revel at Hale Hall, thereat of John Ireland Blackbarne, M.P. Of course there wore the speeches of the usual blood and thunder and never surreinler and die order; and believing that they are the masters of creation, and could " lick," as a Yankee would say, every " critter " eta a cocked hat, their v "

deinonstration all the valiant characterihtics customarily demonstrated on the occasion. One has become accustomed to look forward to a rumpus in connection with them July celebrations: and this year the pugilistic bumps of the fighting party have been developed to the usual degree both in Liverpool and :it. Helens. In St. Ilelem the loyal and orderly body of thangemen must of necessity be conducted in regal fashion, on their arrival in town from the scene of revol, to their various habitations by bands of music.
