At the meeting of the Barracks Committee, held on the 13th inst., the committee vieited the various rooms of the establishment, and found them in a satisfactory condition. Tbe doctor was in attendance, and reported the children to be inn healthy state. lie had inspected the whole of them in order to ascertain whether coy required to be vaccinated. The Rend. Yonge directed the attention of the committee to the public inconvenience and annoyance caused by the each which followed the band on the evenings of the 29th and 30th ult. while parading the town for the purpose of advertising the Workhouse trip. The bandmaster explained that he received instructions to take the band through the principal streets by ao order from the Trip Committee through the secretary, and that such had been the custom for many years past. The Schools Committee, however, thought it desirable that in future the band should not go out after working hours without the Board's sanction, except for the purpose of playing in Bank Park. Major CARTWIIIiiHT moved the adoption of the minutes, and Mr. BROWN seconded the motion. Major Canrwittoirr said he was sorry to observe that out of 2311 children at the Barracks they happened to have a in the workhouse hospital. Mr. Bennis. 51 children sick . . .

—....--. ...... Major CARTWRIGHT said that was so. He had been through the hospital that morning, and he was prepared to prove to the Board that the Barracks were unhealthy. He Was prepared to give his reasons. Even that week on ex- amining the children one was sent front the hospihil on Wednesday supposed to be cured, but was ordered back on Tuesday simply because the disease had broken out again. He declared, and was positive of it, that the place was not a healthy place, ! and from a statement made by the doctor he believed that gentleman was of opinion that it was rote fit place for the children unlem they had some alteration, and that before tong. His opinion wasthat whatever alteration the BoariTmade they could not make the Barracks suitable. It was almost impossible to make it suitable for the number of children the Board had now. Mr. Winstanley might shake his head. Mr. WINSTANI.EI : II WAS you who shook your head, and I came to the conclusion there was nothing in it. (Laugh- ter.) MAIO4 CARTWRIGHT dared say that was very witty on Me. Winstanley's part, bat it was already proved from the num- ber of children sent up. There were six children ordered to the hospital the previous day, but three of them only had been sent. There was, he must say, a great deal of stublorn- nese on the part of the officialsat the Barracks in not sending the children up when they were ordered by the medical officer. The order for those children was given on Tuesday at eleven o'clock, but ouly three of them came the previous night. If they had had the whole number of children sent they would have had Mmn the hospital. The Board had •ever had anything like it before in his experience. and the medical officer would bear him out that they 113tI never bad such sickness amongst the children since he had been a mem- her of that Board-20 years. After hearing the doctor's report they would come to the conclusion that the place was totally ' unfit for the children. Those were positive statements which he could prove, as he did not go tbery and make statement! wlthnoo :' Prone Client So long as the Board had a healthy place at the workhouse, a place they could put the children in without env expense he Must say it was the healthiest place in in Warrington—and without any inconvenience whatever, they had no right to swim those children to supply the hospital with a nutnber of inmates. lie did not know whether the doctor had made a report, but he promised to , make one. The doctor said the dining-room wan not lit to dine in for when the children had been there a few minutm the air became very str mg indeed ; and, in point of fact, there was not room even for less than the 51 children they had in the hospital. At that Workhouse they had a spacious place with a room in which three times the number could dine, and so long as the Board IVO a place there which was fit for the children, and which was healthy, they had no right to keep the children there to breed ilkcase. Ile hoped notice would be taken of the matter, and that an investiga- tion would be made of the Barracks as to whether it was a healthy place add tit for the children. The CHAIRMAW stated that the doctor said a while ago he never remembered 40 few children being ill. Now there were 239 children. and 54 of them appeared to he affected , by some disease of the head. Mr. Ham, remarked that there really most Ire something in what Mejnr Cartwright said as they had bail an instance of it at the Newlin Relief Committee. A man's children were sent to the Workhouse school M a healthy state, but when they came out, after being in a week or two, they ' were affected with the disease.

ws,v The CHAIRMAN said they were all aware that would occur ' even out of that institutiou. (Hear, heard He thought there was more diScase yowled by inattention to the children than by the institution Itself. Mr. WALLING-row said Major Cartwright was very anxious for the children to go to the Barracks. Somehow or other be had changed, and now he was anxious that they should come hack again, and he took every opportunity of bringing it before the Bond. lie was sorry to say Major Cartwright anagnitied everything. Just now lie said that the doctor said the dining-room was not fit to dine in, that it was not Mil- ! Met to hold them all at once. It was never the intention ! of the committee that the children should dine altogether, . but at two sittings; and if they did not tarry that recom- mendation out they did wrong. The disease was a mere akin disease, and lie did not believe the Barracks were on-, healthy. It was a temporary arrangement, and there was the temporary inconvenience attending it, and they should ' Alt magnify its defects, but do what they could to make it perfecf• Mr. WlsrevaXanv said it W. very irregular and very in- I convenient to raise that sort of a discussion without due , notice, bathe for one should not at all object ton committee of any sort being appointed to go into the whole suldsct, ‘M. what evidence they could, and report to the Board. 4Hear, hear.) Ile should be very pleased indeed if that coarse was taken, but he must strongly object to the otatements made from time to time by Major Cartwright, especially when he wanted to bring the children back to that Uwe when he knew very well they could not possibly some. The Board had not anything like the room they hail— eQuestion,"and"Plenty")—and no one knew that better than ' Major Cartwright. The certificate that wtr originally given I at to the number of persons that house was suitable for and ! capable of holding was got under totally different chem. stances to what were existing now. When the house Wail built the Poor Law Board was in its infancy. They were introducing the new Poor Low Amendment Bill, and they met with very great oppomition and very great difficulty.ond the rules that obtained were not near so stringeot at that time as they bad been since, consequently the certificate given of the capacity of that house at that time was very much larger than it would be now. What was the result et the system that was in existence then? Major Cartwright ought to brow, because he was there at the time, but none of the other members betides himself were. At the time hewn, speaking of the boys were allowed to sleep two in abed; hence the nor- tificate was larger on that account. But what was the result? Why, euch a horrible state of things obtained in that house that they were obliged to smother it to prevent it going abroad to the world, which would have been a disgrace to the Union and to Warrington. Major Canrwritour ! I deny it. Mr. WINSTANLET said Major Cartwright's denial would • not alter it. An enquiry took place, a Government inven- tor came down, and the Board were recommended to build a new wing, not for the purpose of receiving an augmented number, but to provide for the number they then had in the house. They could only separate the children by put. hug them into separate beds—and Major Cartwright ought to know that, because he was aware of it at the time—and be knew perfectly well that the capacity of the house was nothing like sufficient to receive MO more inmates. Major CADTWIIIONT : tray it is. 'Mr. HARDISON thought the matter brought before them by Major Cartwright was very important. Ile thought it was far too serious to pass over flippantly, and he hoped no gentleman of that Board would do so. He said that no less than 50 children had been brought to that howse in a elate of disease. Mr. Wallington described it as a mere superficial kind of disease, but he thought they ought to view it in a very different light Indeed. It was a very diffi- cult thing indeed to get rid of it, and, therefore, Ile did not think it Humid be treated as a superficial attack. Petted no feeling whatever in the matter. He supported the child- ren going 001 10 the barracks. It wt, trne, however, to certain point he oppoired them with Major Cartwright, but when he found they must take the Barracks, and that a Local Government Board inspectorwent over the Barracks and said they were suitable, and aso addition they were fortified by the report of the medical officer' it led him to think that the Barracks were suitable: but he heard with some eurpriee that the medical officer said the Barracks were not euitablo. 11 that was so let the medical officer put an end to it arat stop what must certainly become a public ecandal. heard Was it true or wee it not true? Was Major Cart- wright influenced by some personal feeling—[Major CEDE. WRIONT No.)—or (rem a dente to benefit others. He could not believe that Major Cartwright would take up sueh a coarse and act in this nutter on account of spleen. Major Cartwright must be well aware that he had mite a very • Serious charge indeed, and it behoved that Board at once without delay to appoint a committee of enquiry to sea whether it was true or not. But the first thing they should do was to take the opinion of the medical officer and ask hint if he, as medical officer, recommended them to maintain those children at the Barracks or did he condemn them as unsuitable and until tor their reception. It was a scandal for no lees than Id children Cube brought to that House. Mr. BOWDEN rose more particularly to take up a remark that Major Cartwright made use of that morning with

reference to one of the children going from the hospital to the Barracks and the dim., breaking out again. He thought the Board could do no better thing than make an enquiry with reference to the hospital. His own opinion was that the hospital was a sundal to the Board. He , thought it would be well to have . .quiry, because it struck him that the canes were sent back front the hospital not cured, and it being an infection. disease they were spreading it instead of stopping it. He begged to meve— , " That an enquiry be made into the condition of the Bar- ' racks, and also into the management of the Workhouse that the opinion of the other medical men be taken; that the Work- house Medical Officer be requested to make a written re- port on the whole subject from the period of the removal to , the Barracks. and elm to report on the existence of similar ailments of the children in former years." fir. SPINet was compelled to come to the conclusion that! , (here wan something very radi.lly wrong at the Barracks. The members would bear in mind that the Harraelle wren, , never built as barracks but simply as stores, and they would remember when the militia came up—to the number of from IMO to 1,100 men—their permnal clothing was stored in that place. There was no doubt about it that the Barracks were very productive of vermin in the children's heads and clothing, and he could only account for it from the fact that the place was thoroughly unfit for them. 'lle did not think whatever the Board did it would be altered, and he , concluded the s.rner they got the children away front there the Uttter. ( Hear, heard They could not keep the children clean, and he had never sent a child down there but what wa;,11,d17.1.11,1y.a,u.dv pzfieicttlL cared. d torn stated that morning! that some children went down from the house, and were' only away two days, when they came back covered with I vermin. Could that he the result of the bad tie?
—Dr. SPIN. did not see that it wae the result of bad air,' but of dirty walls and dirty floors. : Mr. : 1/o you wish us to understand that there are lice in the floors and walls ?

Dr. Singes said he did not no; but it was there. Ile' would not sleep • night in the place. Mn. BROWN said after the statement he heard on Tuesday he made up his mind that the children should be remove.' —and that as quickly 83 possible— from the Barracks to the Workhouse. If there was no room there to accommodate the, inmates he should suggest that some old men and women should be removed from that house to the Barracks, asthey would not be so liable to the influence of the atmosphere and light as the children were. Mr. WINSTANLEY seconded the motion that a committee be appointed to investigate the matter. Mr. WALLINOTON supported the motion, and disputed the truth of the statetnent about children coming from the Bar., racks swarming with vermin. tie asked any of the Guardians whe.thcr...thee had seen it. . . .

Mr. Woort at r mentioned a case that was brought before the Board at the last meeting by Mrs. Mackey. Mr. °wan said he was positive under the existing rules handed to the Board be the Local Government Board there was plenty of room in the house for all the children. Mr., Pennington and himself had measured the house, hut indepen- dently he found there was plenty of room to accommodate all the children and more emotes. _

- The CHAIHMANaand he new on the Btli March lir. Spinks, in reporting to the Barracks Committee, did not state that the children had been at all affected with the skin disease by their being removed to the Barracks, but on the contrary he was of opinion that the cause of the outbreak of the skin disease was the insufficiency of vegetable diet during the winter season. Ile thought they should direct the doctor to make a written report to the committee which might be ap- pointed. fie feared if the children were brought from the Barracks and put with the children at the Workhouse they would not be any better off, as they had the children isolated now. It had not been shown that the Barracks were the cause of the disease, or if the children had been at the house thedisease would not have broken out.

Majw CARTWRIGHT thought it came with very bad grace from a new member of the Board to make such allu- shins as Mr. Bowden had made. In April last that gentle- man was elected, as they remembered, and he did not think he had been through the house twice, Oct lie was of opinion that there was something wrong in the hospital here. He (Major (artwright) declared he did not think there eras an hospital in the whole of the Lancashire unions that was in a better state than their hospital was. Mr. WINSTANLEII : Pont prejudice the enquiry. The CHAIRMAN : I don't think, gentlemen, we are gaining anything. Major CARTWRIRI, said it eras a reflection upon the chairman of the Visiting Committee, and alsu upon the nurse, and he declared that there was cola single fault to be found the previous Friday. The Chairman was there, and he was surprised he did not make a remark as to what oc- curred. They found everything in proper order, and he had a right to stand op and defend the hospital as chairman of . the House Committee; and when everything was satisfac- ; tory, and any attack was nade upon the officials or anyone poineeted with them—and there was any necessity for it— he should stand up and defend them. He was very glad the Board had come to the conclusion of having s committee to enquire into the matter: ae he bad not the slightest doubt at regarded the result. Dr. Spines said he did not take the remarks as any reflic- then upon him, because he found new members were the only men who could find fault. Ile had been medical officer for nearly 27 years, and such had never lieen said of him before. But as the gentleman was a new member, be did not think anything about it. In regard to the report in March, at that time he thought the disease was owing to the diet, but since then the children have been thoroughly well supplied with vegetables, Ac. The CHAIRMAN thought all those things might be em- bodied in • written report. that rYouW'ClTeTirit HZ% da"vte'rr; ylfeatulttho;dl7llr and well ventilated.
SPINII3 remarked that the children's health vise generally good. Major C1131,111,1NT said the appointment of a committee. w a.s. a reflection on the medical officer. ... . I

Mr. BOWllltti NM! he bad made no pertional attack upon I the doctor. He spoke in reference to the general manage- I ment of the hospital, and he begged to remind Major , Cartwright that he WAS quite as competent ea he or any other member to judge of acts in that house no far as he ' understood and saw them. Ile had a perfect right to give his opinion, and, as Major Cartwright had said himself in defence of the same principle, to stand up and introduce a subject to that Board at any time he thought desirable, and he should do so without asking the permission of Major Cartwright. Major CAPTIVIIIOICI , I shall never object. Mr. Bownusr: I think your remarks are very uncalled for. I The resolution was then carried.

div.head: MN BOARD RESOLVE TO PETITION AGAINST THE GOTEEN-
div.p: MN BOARD RESOLVE TO PETITION AGAINST THE GOTEEN-

Mr.PENNINGTON, in accordance with notice of motion, rose to move" that a petition from the Board be sent against the Bill now before Parliament to alter the Vaccination acts," and in so doing mid he felt so interested on the subject that he could notation- it to pass without endeavouring to oppose the alteration of the laws. The benefits he had received from vaccination in his own family, gave him very great reason for asking the Board to petition against the proposed , alteration,., his experitnce entitled him to my that vaccina- Bop was a great benefit. If it was a had law let it be re- , pealed, but if it was a good one it should be enforced. Mr. Owen seconded the motion. .. •

------- ...—...... Mr. ,lALL proposed an amendment that a petition be for- warded in favour of the Bill, and quoted figures to show that on the Continent the number of vaccinated persons who died from moan pox exceeded that of the unvaccinated perwns. He said that no person with a conscience would consent to persons who conscientiously refused to allow their children to he vaccinated, being persecuted in the way they were at present. Mr. Bownss seconded the amendment Co that the matter could be discusswl.

Mr. HARRISON said be would be exceedingly sorry if the I Board of Guardians degraded itself by petitioning in favour of the Bill brought in by Her Majesty's Government. A more retrograde measure it woe impossible to conceive, and bow anv Government could bring in a Bill to divot,so with cumulative penalties he could not for his its imagine. It was a just principle, and ,just for this reason. that every re- filial of a man^lio have his child vaccinated was a fresh offence, and carried with it fresh consequences. It was no injustice to a man who wilfully and perversely objected to have his child vaccinated an, more than it was to say that a man who had been fined for drunkenness should not be fined again. It would be the greatest mistake that could potieibly he made if tlioy did anything to relax the stringency of the law as it now existed for the purpose of securing the vaccination of every child born in England. It was proved that vaccination had been productive of untold good, and anything done to relax the etringeney of the lawn would be a national misfortune. Mr. WINFITMen said he was sorry the matter had ever been seriously opposed, because he agreed with Mr. Harri- son that it would be a reflection upon their intelligence if they did anything to lumen what he believed to be one of the greatest aaleguards that could possibly be introduced. The amendment was then put, and two members viced in favour of it and 12 members against. The motion was there- fore carried that the Board petition against the Bill. This concluded the business of public interest.

ABANDON/L., OF A RusTconw Broor.—The steamer Wellington, returning from Southport to Blackpool on the night of the 9th Sid,, fell in with an abandoned sloop drift- ing on shore. Two men were placed on board, and the Wellington proceeded to Blackpool tel landed the pamengera. She then returned, and towed the derelict M Lytham. It was apparent that the sloop had posed through a severe ! storm as her meet was gone. She proved to be the Princes. Royal, of Runcorn. bound from Barrow to Pit ton Brook, with iron ore. The Princess Royal was owned he Captain John Millinger, of Wellingtonmtreet, Runcorn, who, with Lie son manned the vessel. She left Barrow about eight o'clock on Thursday morning, with iron ore consigned to the Ditton Brook Iron Company. There mace heavy sea on at thetime the mind blowing west. They proceeded all right until shout foar o'clock in the afternoon. When opposite Black- pool. about five or six mile. from land, the vessel began to labour very heavily, and the mast broke off about 90 feet shove the deek. Rhe became quite unmanageable. and the two men on board were placed in an exceedingly dangerous position. The whoener Margaret Ann, of Barrow. Captain ' James Lee, coming up at the time, and Captain Millinger seeing that no good could be done by remaining with the ship, especially as night was approaching, detamined to leave his vessel to her fate and proceed to Liverpool with the passing easel. Accordingly the boat was launched And Captain Millinger and his son rowed to the Margaret Are. and arrived in Livertmol about ten o'clock the same night. The vessel was not insured.

Smoot-ea Can.—An elderly man named Creorge Aaron. elan excitable temperament, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, on the sth inst.. at Weston. P.C. Jackson . said he was on duty in Weston village, on the night of the bth net , when he saw the defendant drunk, canning a dis- turbance, and in the act of atri king a Irian. Defendant had his coat off. Vrii asking Aaron Dr his name, he gave it to him.—Mr. Lake (Messrs. Day and Lake, appeared for the defence, and said that the officer had been misled by the I defendant being under very great excitement, and laving a slight impediment in his speech. On the night in queation Aaron was in the Round-house public bowie, and • man named Rubinson began chaffing him about his wife, stating I that she :was not truthful to him and unduly intimate with her lodger, which naturally excited the defendant very much. When the house closed, at tea o'clock, he went to his own door, which was next to the house.and whilst standing there Robinson came up, and again teased and jeered him. During the conversation Robinson said he would go to his (defen-. , dent's) house and get lodgings, alter which "precious little of the husband he would In,' upon which Aaron struck Robinson. Defendant had been at sea some years, and had contracted a somewhat rolling gait, which might have de- : ceived the officer.—Defendant was called, and in answer to I Inspector Dutton, he said he was in the public house from half past seven o'clock at night. —John l'adbury and Joseph Talbot, both labourers, were called 'to prove that the defendant was sober.—Mr. Lake said his client had been in the Racy for several years, and he handed to the magistrates his dis- charge, which stated that he had always been a temperrte man in his habits, lie also showed the bench a note front the defendant's foreman stating that he had worked nine months under him and not lost any time—The Chairman said the Bench were of opinion that tbe police officer had done his duty very properly in summoning Aaron, but, at the same time, they thought lie (defendant) had had great provocation. In May of last year he was acting am clerk to Mr. Woml at Salford, and on the Bth of Om month the prisoner came to Lim to ask if he could hire a boat horse for his own use. He arranged with the prisoner to hire a grey horse at 30s. lon. period of four weeks. Prisoner signed an agreement after it had been read over to him. gave Ititet IRA address, and said that he worked for Mn. Joseph Davie, coal and salt merchant. of Ituncorn.—Wni. Schofield, manager to the prosecutor, said he received tire letters produced by post from the pri- soner. Mr. Davies had not agreed to pay for the hire of the animal.—Mr. James Delaney raid he worked foe Mr Davies, and the prisoner had been in the employ of his toaster eight or nine months. Ile was working for them in May, feat year, and on the 15th December, 1879. he purchased the grey horse from him. At the time named Lomb was in the debt of Mr. Davies to the amount of £2 17s. 3d. He was inrtructe.d by his master to get the horse for the debt. He accordingly threw up Cr agreement, which the prisoner signed, he representing the horse to be his, They had never written to Mr. Wood stating that they would be responsible for the hire—P.C. Hilbert proved apprehending the pri- soner on the previous Thursday in Nelson-street, on which he raid "It's Davies that should Ire in this trouble, not me." --Mr. Lewin appeared for the defence, and cross-examined the witness Delaney at great length.—Witness, on being closely pressed, said he could not meat that the prisoner said the horse was his own, but he entered into negotiations for its sale as if it were. The horse had since died, and the money obtaiaed for the sale of the carcase-Bs. 6d.—went to Mr. Davies. When begot the prisoner to sign the agree- ment he made the observation to him It is only a matter of form." Ile believed that of the £2 17s. 31 the prisoner owed El for stable charges. there was no case, and eaid that Mr. Delaney had contra. dieted himself in the evidence which he had given that day as compared with that he tendered on Saturday. .-TIIII-61:1;11;;;ZOT..;;;;;.THADS.—On Thursday a number of bonds engaged in the soiling-room left their employment in consequence of the refusal of the employers to advance wages 5 percent. The strike will only be, partial one, a number of hands having been induced to withdraw their notices to leave. There area number who still bold out, and these, acting on the resolution of a meeting held in the Temperance Hall, are determined to go on strike. Iris Hated on the authority of the Employers' Association, that thereare only three mills in the borough where the whole of the strippers and grinders and the female cardroom hands have given notice to leave. OFENINO OF NEW SCEIOOI.II.—F.ErI Spencer and Mr. Munitella on Thursday opened the Central Schools at Sheffield. The schools, which, with the Board offices, have been erected at a cost of 250,000, will be devoted to the higher education of whirlers drafted front the public elementary schools. Earl Spencer, in opening the schools, referred to the advantage, to be Serived in central schools by the training of pupil teacher, and also the importance of technical education, which would be of great are in a manu- facturing community. The School Board had, he said, shown their interest in education in many ways, doing a noble work in carrying cat the Education Act of tag, in primary schools, and lo completing the work of the elementary education by providing the Central Schools. FARMERS FINED FOR RAILWAY BeFIDIERN—AE Congleton, George and Joseph Proctor, farmers, were brought up on tho charge of having stolen a number of felt hats, elle property of the the North Stafford Railway Company' On April 111th last, a crate containing felt hats, addressol to a London consignee, got thrown off • track when the train Wan travelling, and fell on the embankment adjoining a field on the farm of the last named prisoner. When the crate was found by some of the company's officials it was dis- covered that a numbo of hate had been abstracted. In consequence of Geo. Proctor having been seen to give away a number of hats as presents, suspicion attached to him, anal on hie house being searched 14 new hats similar to those left in the crate were found, and also four in another house. These were identified by the consigner, James Wolfenden, of Denton, as forming part of the property coneigned to the railway company. It appears that several hate had been given away, trimmed and worn, in one case the elder mison- er's daughter having chosen "a black hat for every day, awhile one for bog, and a grey one to wear when she went to market.' Joseph Proctor was tined .Cl 5 and George .ClO. Roberts, proprietor of the Brookland Copper Works, gave hie annual treat to his employes in the form of an excursion to Soothport, on Saturday morning, when over sixty persons, including the wires and sweethearts of the employed, went to that place from Sr. Helens 1-v as ordinary morning train. FARIEII CITURCII St-finev Scwoote.—This annual trip took place on Monday, when about 300 went by • train leaving St. Helens at 6-15 am. to Bangor. The train consisted of fifteen carriages, the' Rev. Dr. Car, the Hon. Mrs. Carr, the Rev. Mr. klermagen, with others. accompanying the excursionists in a saloon carriage. Many of the excursionists alghted at Rhyl and Llandudno, but the bulk went to Bangor, arriving at that place soon after nine o'clock. The excursionists left Bangor at a few minutes before seven, and arrived at Ft. Helens at eleven o'clock. -

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of the above authority teas held in the Beard-room, at the Workhotiae, Dutton, on Tuesday. Present :—The Rev. Canon Barclay (in the chair), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs Wilkinson, Mclntyre, Pollard, J. Ashton, Smith, sen., Derbyshire, liighnelJ,Reild, Mkhrood, and H. Linaker clerk ). TEC OFFICE.' QUARTERLY ESTURNS.

[Sr. VI, illett reported that the mortality retutn for the Great Budworth district for the quarter ending 30th June was 12. Three were returned for April, 7 for May, and 2 for June-5 being males and 7 females. One child died under 5 years the average of the rest would he 4311 yeam. The total birth, for the mine period was 33, malm2o,and females 13. Six deaths were returned during the quarter for the Dareshury diatrict (two in each month), 3 male. and 3 females, and a total birth return of 12 (4 in each month I, 8 males and 8 females. One chikl died under 5 years; the remainder mainhtined an average of 41 years. Measles were were prevalent amongst children in the Great Budworth district during the months of April and May, hut fortunately without a single death. Every pesaible sanitary measure was adopted. Stratton as usual woe the principal infected quarter which necemitated the entire clotting of the school. for several weeks. Both schools were thoroughly lime washed, and disinfected, before the children re-assembled, Bo far these precautions bad apparently proved effectual, and they had not had a recurrence of the disease. No other contagious dimase had ',reveled during the quarter, and at the preaent time he was pleased to observe that the health of the two districts was exceedingly satisfactory.— Dr. Weaver reputed that during the quarter ending 30th June there were in the Frodsliain division 72 births, 40 males end 32 female.. The deaths were 12, 7 males and 5 females. The death-rate of the quarter was 72 per 1,000 (per year), a remarkably low rate. The district was at pre- sent nearly free form contagious epidemic disease—Dr. Carruthers reported that during the quarter ending June, 1880, the registrars' returns recorded 38 births and 28 deaths in the Balton and Weston district. Of the births 12 were males and 2rl to pales. Of the deaths 15 were males and 13 females. Four were under One years of age (two of theae being tinier one year), and 24 were five yea. and upwards. The Authority then proceeded to consider the appoint. mente of medical officersof health Each meniber had been served with a notice, but the following minute was recorded at the last meeting The clerk reinindsl the Authority that the appointments of the ININIICAI officers of health would terminate on the 29th September next, and directed attention to a letter from the Local Covernment Board, dated 20th August lace, recommending the Authority to sp. paint one medical officer of health for the rural sanitary district of the Union, or to enter Into • combination with the authorities of some adjoining district for the purpose of a joint appointment of such 1112 officer." The CHAIRMAN said before the appointment of the pre- sent district medical oflicers there was a great deal of die. cusaion on the eubject, and it waa thought that the best plan would be to appoint a medical officer for the whole of the union and an adjoining union, so that he could devote the whole of his time to the duties of the office, and not have private practice. That, however, was overruled, partly on the ground of expense, and partly, he had no doubt, owing to their kindly feelinge towards the present medical officers of the Union, and from the idea that they were underpaid. He would like the Authority to underetand that the present step which they were bound to take wee not because they thought any less of their medical officers, but because it had been brought under their notice by the Local liovernment Board. Their medical officers hail always tlone their duty, and he did not remember a single one or any accusation of neglect having been brought against them. Ile thot.ght if the Authority made any other arrangement by which the Union would combine with another, and their present medical officers were deprivetl of their dutiee, that it was not becauee that Authority was dissatisfied with them. The OAR& said he got information from four other Union& which ehoweal that in Altrinchani, Northwich, and Tarvin the medical officer of health was appointed for • combined district of Sanitary Authorities. In Ormskirk that was not the case. The proportions paid by each Authority were—Altrincharn, £209 per annum; Northwich, £164 ; and Tarvin, £lOB. In Ormskirk the total annual salary was £137 10s, for live officers; in Runcorn. for three officers at £5O each, £l5O. In all cases a portion of the salary was paid from the parliamentary grant,. The area of the Altrincham district was 85,578 acres ; Northwich, 45,0(0) acres; Ormskirk, 70,705 acre.; Tarvin. 47,058 acres; and Runcorn, 45,241 acres. The populatione in 1871 were —Altrinchani, 28,059; Northwich, 11,540; Ormskirk, . . 22,493; Tarvin,.ll,3B3 and Runcorn, 17,953. •"

..,-- Sir, i,ANSET,'io;pectr to the Local Government Board, said he had no doubt the medical officers in the Union dis- charged their duties properly. He had no fault to find with , them. Their reports had always come to hand ion proper manner, and their shale. had been discharged satis- factorily to the Local Government Board. But their experience on the whole had proved that the working of the Public Health Act by Poor Law medical officers had not generally been satisfactory, as their private practice bad wmewhat interfered with their Poor Low duties. lie did not care how honourable a man might be, he could not but be influenced by a private feeling. He was hound to have some feeling if he had a private feeling, and the Local Government Board had thonght it expedient for lone man to devote the whole of his time to the duties, and have no private practice whatever. Of course alarge Ada'y would tie expected for a medical man to give up his private practice, but that would be on the unlerstanding that his , work would extend over a large area. In Cheshire they had soveral combinations, and he ,night mention that they had the Cliester,'Parvin, and Wirral rural sanitary authorities, and the Chester and Neston and Tarporley urban district. The popu• lation of the Chester rural district was 8.241, the acrffige 38,016, and they paid £B6 per annum, half of which was re- , paid by the Loyal Government Board. The Taffiin rural authority had a population of 11,000 or a little over, and an acreage of 47,060, and they paid £lOB per annum, half of ' which was repaid by the Local Government Board. The Wirral unitary district hail a population of 12,156, with an arrant 34,037 acres, and they paid £127 per year, half of which woe repaid. The Chester authority had a population of 35,000, with an arta much smaller than any of the others. They paid £240 per year, half of which was repaid. The Neaten and Tarporley Local Boards had small districts, and they paid .C3O per year each, making a total of /WO per year paid to the medical officer. He then referred to the letter of the Local Government Board, doted 231 h August, in which they urged upon the Guardians the expediency of giving the matter their careful consideration, and submit tbent any proposal which they thought proper, either for ionthination with an adjoining district, or for the appoint- ment of such an officer. He could not tell exaffily what the cost would be to the Union if they combined, but probably it would be about £l5 or £2O lest than they at present p dd. What the Authority might pay would net be added to the medical officer's salary, but would go towards decreasing the amount paid by other unions in which they combined. He hail to point out that two or three delegates would have to be appointed to attend a meeting to discuss and Nettle the question of salary. term of office, and other details. The Local Government Board would issue an order tarn combination.
The CHAIRMAN asked if the propoml which Mr. Dansey had mentioned would not make the work to much for ono °Men ?
Darr•dre slid not think so and instanced larger diatricta than that in which one man did the whole of the work.

The CHAlexem cud it seemed to him that If the medical officer receivol a couple of letters in the someday, one asking him to go to the extreme end of Wirral, and the other telling him to go to the extreme end of Bedworth, it would be a long time before one of then) was attended to. Mr. Dawson mid other districts had worked well. especially one in Shropshire which he might mention was a grett deal larger district than this. lien. J. W. N. TANNER remarked that the railway accom. mmlation was not very good in that district. The CHAIRMAN wished to know on what principle the proportion each Authority had to pay war calculated it Mr. Danny mid that it was considered by the delegates who were appointed and the rateable value was taken into consideration. . .

The Croon asked if there would be any objection to the Runcorn Union being divided into two parts—one part on the west site of the Weaver going to Wirral, and the Bud- worth portion to Altrincham. Mr. Bawer, said that he did not know any district which bad been divided into two parts, and could not say whether the Local Government Board would a:low it. If the Authority did not combime with come other union they would have to pore man who would devote hi, whole time to the duties. It would be an outrageous expense which the Union could not bear, so that the easiest way to meet the matter would be to combine with another district. . . . . .

Rev. J. W. N.ANN. moved the following resolution ! "That this Authority combine with certain other Saniisry Authorities for the purpose of securing the aervices ef an independent medical officer for the whole of the district." Mr. Wilt:rime seconded theresolution,which was carried.

Mr. PoNSFT said the Local Government Boar had re- ceived from the Authority copy of resolutions parsed at a meeting of the ratepayers of Frodsham Lordship. They would remember that on the 2.lth May the Local Govern- ment Board asked the Authority to re-consider the subject of sewerage for Frodsham Lordship, and the only reply they had received was thoae resolutions. The Authority did not aay what decision they had arrived at, but simoly enclosed copy of the resolutions passed by the ratepayers. At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Mr. John Migarina the son of a Dillon farmer, was charged with being on the Premime of Mr. Wm. Darlington, of the Four-topped (tali beershop, Dillon. Al two o'clock on the morning of the I 11th instant, for an unlawful purpose. Defendanl. who was represented by Mr. Swift, appeared to feel considerably ashamed of himself. Mary Wilcox, • respectably-dressed and rather go•d- looking young woman, about eighteen years of age, said alle was servant to Mr. Darlington, and about two o'clock on the morning in question she heard someone in her bedroom, where she was sleeping with a girl named Nfergaret McDer- mott. She asked who wet there, but received no answer, and, after waiting about five minutes, she heard a second ntorement, and called her mistress, upon which the man decamped.

--Sergeant Comte said hewer in the oeiglshourboal of the prosecutor's house on the morning of the 11th inst., at two o'clock. He saw the prisoner in Doke-street, Ditton. The house of the prosecutor was about a quarter of • unite from the prfkoner's. The young man wart dressed just es he then appeared in court. Mr. Swift said that even presuming that their woe. ships thought the case made out to their satisfaction that the prisoner was the MAO, there did not appear to bare been anything beyond some freak on his part, or possibly, lie had nude a mistake, having had drink, o doubt their worships were aware that the s. unlawful purpose" could only be properly established by evidence, and it must be evidence pointing to scone intention to commit crime— not merely to do • civil wrong, or commit a trespass. It sets quite likely that as the prisoner was under the influence of drink, he might hare thought he was going into his own house when he entered the chamber, bat, at all events, he did not appear to hare had any intention of resorting to any violence. The " un- liwful purpose" moat be the commission of some offence, which if provod, would cause the prisoner to be committed, —such as stealing, and not simply an AM of immorality.— Mr. Swift then quoted from " (ke's Magisterial Synopsis " as to shut muet be understood by the term "unlawful pur- pose." The prisoner seemed to have found out that he was in the wrong place, and us soon as he mails this diacovery he vanished. At that time it was distinctly understoo;l that he gave a promise to leave the neighbourhood and go to some place where he would Iry to behave himself in a respectable manner. div.head: ORANGE DISTURBANCE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ORANGE DISTURBANCE AT ST. HELENS.

The I.?th of Jule was observed by the Orangemen of St. Helens taking part this year in the grand demonstration at Hale Park, lent for the ocention by the junior metnber for South-West Lancashire, Colonel J. Ireland Blackburne. The members of the 0 Prince of Orange," the "Earl of Derby," and "St. Helens Glory" lodges mustered at the George Inn, Water-street,and marched to the railway station, headed by the Pmsley Cross Brass Band. The ntembet of the" Ellis- killen Glory "neat in vehicles afterwards, and were in time to form the demonstration. be first-nanted lodges pro- ceeded to Hale Bank by rail. Speeches were delivered con- demning the action of the present Government on several points, the adroinsion to Parliament of Mr. Bradlaugh toeing one of the questions dwelt upon. Arrived back at St. Helens a Alight disturbance took place, at about seven o'clock, which was repeated a few times later on. It ap- pears front what we can gather that the members of the va- rious lalges were comlucted by the band to their respective lodge rooms, and a crowd gathered round the processionists an they wended their way through the streets. Having taken one of the lodges" home.'' they were escorting some other brothers itt like manner, when a woman in the crowd, evidently disposed to create a breach of the peace, interfered with the musical functions ef the big drummer by striking the drum with her fist. The man who wielded the drum stick desisted, wisely or unwis•ly, we will not say, in his endeavours to create "concords of musical sounds ' and devoted his attention and drumstick to the sroman's cranium, and unfortunately "knocked" the fair one and the bind considerably out of tune. The result Man that the roughs, willing at all times for a little excite- ment, took great delight in the pares, and resorted lover,, effective means to cot tinue it mortar or. Helens style: and if Mr. Matthew Arnold could only have been a witness to the mode of fighting which was adopted on this °cession, he would have been more and more confirmed that to, opinion of St. Helens being a "hell-hole "in a correct one. However, the way in which the mob tested the calibre of certain individuals' physiognotnies and lower extremities calls for the contletnnation of every respectable man or wo- man in the tow n, be he or she an affintrer of King William the Third, or one strongly opposed to turn and alt his works From the descriptions °Hite doings of the crowd given loon, reporter, and from what he saw himself, "there is indeed much satisfaction to the instinct in man for expansion but little satisfaction to his instinct for a fit and pleasing form of social life and manners." A young fellow named Grime, a cornet player in the Peasley Cross bram band, was knocked down, kicked, and reodered ninon- Stone.throwing then commenced, several people being hit, but, the police coming on the some, about this time, they partially dispersed the crowd, and the band proceeded home from the fury of the mob. Some of the members of the police had seen some stone-throwing, and wren eager in the execution of their duty to arrest the delinquents, but the crowd scampered away in all directions, the police chasing about a hundred of them through the yard of SOrrle chemical works in Parr and also up Langtree- , street, but no one was taken into custody. This toeing an opportunity for an attack upon the police, stones were thrown at them, and one member woe hit on the leg, the effects of which he felt for some time after. Whilst this was going rein the Parr end of the town, Liverpool.road was alive with hundreds of people, who bad been attracted be mine boisterous individuals who had more fire and combativeness in their beings than logic in their brains. Consequently there were several scnilles, which developed in magnitude as the Gine went on and the crowd increased. The number of people in the street may be gathered from a remark which a policeman made afterwards to the effect that he could see a brother-officer's hat about a quarter of a mile up, but he could not get to him. There were only about three or four policemen in that district, and much difficulty was experienced in making the CTOW6.I moos on." One or tan individaale ceahl be rem with fiery indigna- tion flashing from their eye, as they were prevented by their friends from ottling their disputes in a manner beeoming the disciples of Heenan. By the exertions of the constables and of g priest, comparative order was restored in this rPstrict. At the ',anew 01 Etst-ttreek, near to the county court, and in Tontine.streer, there was also Mete , disorder, a man in Tontine-street being struck on the head with a bottle, but ha received no very great injury. The man who inhicted the blow suddenly became aware of the consequences that would ensue if lie stayed in the crowd muck longer, so he took to hie licels—"put his best foot first," as the saying goes—and in less than a minute was beyond the Men of his enemies. In the row which took place in Church-street a young man employed at the Post Office left his work for a moment to alleviate the trouble of aerviagelirldm and on returning to his work he was set upon loy by two or three men, who abused him in such a manner that on the following morning his fare and head presented ever,, swollen appearance. He did the beet he could to defend himself, and, as he describes it, " landed out right and left" for some tinie, but came off much the worse for the encounter, as the looking-glass plainly told the tale next morning. The streets were completely cleared at about ten o'clock.

div.head: ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT HALE
div.p: ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT HALE

On Mondar morning, about 150,090 membem of Orange : lodges left Liverpool for tiarston, front r hence they walked in procession (which was more than two miles in length) to Hale Hill, where Colonel Blackburne, M.P., had kindly placed his beautiful park at their disposal for the by. Be- tween 90 and 100 lolges were represented from Liverpool, twelve lodges pot in an Appearance front Birkenhead, six from Wallasey, three from Southport, three front Whines,l twelve from St. Helens, fourteen from Warrington and On from Prescot.

During the afternoon an opersair meeting woe held, which was presided over bye Mr. Jen-in, who, in the course of his remarks, expressed his regret that some of the gentlemen of Liverpool who bad promised to attend had failed to pot in an appetrance. (Hear, hear.) If the assistance of Orangemen was wanted by those gentlemen for any public purpose, they would be ready to apply to them, cap in hand. (Applause.) Mr. JOSEPH BALL then moved the drat resolution, *Lich was as follows--" That we, a hotly of loyal Orangetnen, as- sembled in public meeting, hereby express our warm sp. prove! of the course adopted by the leader of the Opposition, Sir Stafford Northcote, in the action recently taken to pre- vent the present Government admitting an avowed Atheist into the House of Commons ; and believing the worst anti- cipations from the return of the present Administration to power are being fully realised by the encouragement given to fropgry, in the appointment of the Marquis of Ripon as the Governor-litneral of India, Lord Kenmore as Lord Chamberlain to the Qneen, and Lord O'llagan as Lord Chancellor of Ireland, we call upon all fe.thful and loyal subjects to use their beat endeavours to put such a Ministry out of power, in order to avert further injury to the country and its 6)m-honoured institutions!' Mr. Duo seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously. Mr. E. HARPI,II moved the next resolution, which was as follows That this meeting. taking into consider.ion the efforts mode by the Liberal whip, Mr. Adam (since pro- moted to a Government position), to secure the return as member for Northampton of an intidel, blasphemer, and vendor of inunorsl and seditious publications ; and also the discreditable manoeuvres suboequentiv adopted by Mr. Glad- stone and a certain section of the Liberal party, to thrust I Mtn into the House of Commons without the solemnities re- quired oy ben—termite duty to protest against such con- ' duct as • disgrace to Berish statesmanship and a direct en. Icouragetnent to the propagandists of revolutionary and de. moralising principles among the people."
_ M. Evitatirr iteconded the resoluiioo, which was passed amid cheers.

The Rev. W. DENT-VON proposed the following resolu- tion :—"That this meeting tulle believing. under the g.d providence of tied, this country h.te boon bles..l in genera- ! lions past by. fern adherence to sound Protestant principles, : feels called upon to insist upon the Conservative leader, in I Parliament and others openly to avow their firm determine- I don to resist all Romieh encroachments on our Protestant Constitution, to uphold tha Protestant churches of England and Scotland, to promote .riptural instruction in am public .h.ls, and to put down the Ritualistic conspirsey—the grievances of which the people of England continue to suffer through the perversion of their ahurches to Romish proposm by unfaithful clergyman, and the opposition of certain bishops to the suppression of illegal practises ; that it is the dutv of the authorities in Church and State to enforce the are against such offenders, and if found intro. Strew, to have the law amended, no that there may be preserved to the people their birthright of Christian worship in accordance with God's Word and the Protestant formu- laries of the English Chureb. The Rev. R. If. lhafccar seconded the re.hation, and dwelt at some length mann the danger of admitting Atheists to Parliament. fle added that those present should do their utmost to drive from power a semi-Popish and Atheistical- UtsfendingGovernment. The resolution was carried unanimously.

Mr. G. Fn.-Irk, TOVed the next resolution. It was AS follows:—"That, in the opinion of this meeting, Parlia- mentary candidates should only receive Prote,tant support , when distinct pledgee are given for the mamtenance of !Church. Throne, and Constitution, the integrity of the : British Empire. and the nuppreminn of all movements calm,- : toted to weaken the existing acttlement as established by William the Third of immortal memory that, if this conree had been pursued previous to the gem-rut election, hero would have been a very different remit oad that only in an appeal to the Protestant feeling and Christian patriotism of the nation list the hope of recovering lost ground, and, through the Divine blessing, a restoration to power of those who hove so wiaelv guided the Affairs of this great empire." Mr. BALLARD aeconded the resolution, ood it was agreed to.

The Rev. Mr. Monnow moved the next resolution, which was as follows :—"That we tender to the Right Honourable . the Earl of Beaconsfield our beet thanks for the appointment, I as first Bishop of Liverpool. of the Right they. J. C. Ryle D.P. We pray that his lordship tray yet be spared to mate lother appointments of a like nature. return shortly to the Premiership of this great people, and finish the existing law for the putting down of Ritualism. We also entreat His Lordship the Bishop of Liverpool to use every endeavour to stamp oat the existing encroachments on the time-honoured formularies of the Church of England, and preserve her. as far Is possible. from the subtle enem• now within her pale.' I Mr. W. P. RINGL.,III seconded the resolution, and it was I

OS the motion of the Rev. G ClftioN. seconded by the Roe. W. MORROW, a cordial vote of thanks was passed to !Colonel Blackburne for his kindneas in granting the one of the park. The people referred from the park in the evening to Garston, and thence by train to Liverpool. The weather was splendid throughout the day, but about five o'clock rain began to fall heavily, and continued for several hours.

John Thornhill Harrison, C.E., attended at tire offices of the Widnes Local Board, on Thursday, on behalf of the Local Government Board, for the purpose of enquiring into the application of the Board to borrow L-10,000 in order to carry out works of ttewsge. REFLECTIONS ON SCHOOL EXAMINATIONS. Sir,—With your permission I should like to make a few . remarks on the above subject. At the outset I may say that I quite agree with the remarks of previous writers on this subject. The mode of examining children teat present carried on is far from being on a satisfactory basis. It seems • to be the rule with an inapector —though there are creep- , tions, of course—to fin I out what the children do nnt know, instead of attempting to discover what they to know.
